- Impulse Buying: Why You Buy Stuff You Don't Need: Kind: captions Language: en [INTRO ♪] You’ve probably noticed that in a lot of stores, they make you run through a gauntlet of candy bars, nail clippers, and phone chargers before you can pay and make your escape into the outside world. Maybe you wonder who buys all that stuff. Or maybe you’re already unwrapping a candy bar you had not planned to buy. Those bins are just one of the tricks retailers use to get you to impulse buy, where you purchase something without planning for it in advance. That means you are spending more money than you were originally going to, so you can see why stores would try so hard to get you to do it. But whether their tricks work depends a lot on your personality, and how your brain reacts to perceived gains and losses. Impulse buyers tend to be impulsive in general, which isn’t too surprising. In a 2016 survey of nearly 1500 people, those that said they were likely to spend a hypothetical windfall impulsively also reported higher levels of other impulsive behavior, like binge drinking and unprotected sex. And a lot of psychologists think these choices come down to the same thing: a battle between parts of your brain. One part, called the nucleus accumbens, activates in proportion to how excited you’ll be to have that new thing you want. It’s the same region that activates for what are known as primary reward drives—things like food and sex. Another part of the brain, the insula, has a big reaction to something else: the price. The bigger the price, the more the insula activates. Psychologists call this reaction the “pain of paying” because the insula also activates when we expect to be hurt physically, and when we’re exposed to negative things like horrible smells. Meanwhile, a third region, the mesial prefrontal cortex, also plays a role— it, too, reacts to the price, activating when you think you’ve gotten a good deal. Researchers are able to do a pretty good job predicting whether someone will make a purchase by comparing activation in these three regions. But not everyone’s brain reacts the same way to the same deal, which has led some psychologists to think that we all fall on a spectrum of "pain of paying”— basically, how much spending money bothers us. On one end are the spendthrifts, who just don’t really feel that pain. They think nothing of spending some extra money if they've got it. That’s what it's there for, right? On the other end are the tightwads, who will wait until the last minute to pull out their wallets, even for things they definitely need— for them, the pain of paying is more like the agony of paying. And I know this personally. I sweat, I get hot, I get—my armpits go. It’s, like, the least comfortable I ever am. Spendthrifts are naturally impulsive buyers, and not necessarily because they have more money to spend. A 2007 survey of over 9000 people found those at the spendthrift end of the spectrum had more credit card debt. But even though tightwads don’t like spending money, they’re more vulnerable to certain types of tricks designed to get them spending money they don’t intend to. That’s because they really feel anything that reduces their intense pain of paying. Since spendthrifts aren’t pained anyway, ploys to reduce pain don’t work as well on them. For example, in one 2007 study, researchers asked 538 college students if they were willing to pay a five dollar fee to get overnight delivery on a new purchase. But for half the people, they called it the "small five dollar fee" to reduce the pain of paying. That one word didn't matter to the spendthrifts at all— about the same amount paid the fee either way. But just describing the fee as "small" made the tightwads feel much better about paying the price— about three times as many thought that it was worth it to get the delivery overnighted. What? Excuse me, I have to go make some changes to DFTBA.com. Other research has found a similar effect with using credit cards, which are thought to reduce the pain of paying by keeping the actual, physical money out of sight and out of mind. In a shopping study on 125 students, paying by credit card instead of cash didn't affect the spendthrifts’ buying behaviors at all, but tightwads were more willing to spend money on unhealthy stuff they didn't need. Those candy bar displays don’t really reduce the pain of paying in any way, so they’re probably not the type of trick that will get the tightwads spending more. But sticking a bunch of tempting chocolate in front of the spendthrifts passing through? That might get some cash. Your spending habits may also be influenced by another personality trait— whether you're what psychologists call a "maximizer" or a "satisficer." For maximizers, decision making is never easy. If a maximizer needs a new computer, for example, they might open up a spreadsheet, and find all the computers on the market, and start listing things like price, processor speed, hard drive capacity. They’re gonna watch a bunch of YouTube videos on a bunch of different YouTube channels. They’ll weigh everything that might be important before making their final choice. A satisficer is the kind of person who says, "y'know, I just need something that I can watch YouTube videos on," and they get the first thing that fits that description. In other words, they go with the first thing that satisfies their requirements. It shouldn’t come as a shock that satisficers tend to spend money more impulsively, because they make purchases more quickly than maximizers. But the funny thing is, there's lots of research that suggests that maximizers aren't as happy with what they buy, and they regret their purchases more. It's like, once they put so much thought into that mental spreadsheet of all their options, they have trouble leaving it behind. So making your spending decisions quickly might mean you spend more than you intended, but it isn't all bad. In the end, whether you’re a spendthrift or a tightwad, or a maximizer or a satisficer, there are some things that you can do if you want to check your impulsive spending. If the pain of paying matters to you, you can try ditching the credit cards and paying in cash. Lots of studies show that using cash slows down spending because it forces you to literally watch the money as it’s in your hand and then not anymore. Or, if you see something you think you want, consider waiting before you actually buy it. Understanding that having your hands on something sets off that feel-good reward excitement in your brain might help you resist the urge. Then you can see if you're still thinking about it later on. This has been SciShow Psychology. If you want to learn more about how companies try to hack your brain to maximize sales, you can check out our video on how ads are designed to persuade you. - The Psychology Behind Unnecessary Purchases: Kind: captions Language: en You walk into the Apple store. Your old phone is fine, but the battery is a little slow and the screen has a tiny crack. You convince yourself you need the upgrade. It's for work, right? It's a productivity tool. So, you drop $1,200 on the new iPhone Pro Max Titanium. You walk out of the store feeling good. You feel successful. But then you get into your car and you look at the phone. It's sleek. It's futuristic. And suddenly your old frayed charging cable looks like garbage next to it. It feels wrong to plug this masterpiece of engineering into a $5 gas station cable. So you buy the new MagSafe charger. That's $40. Then you get home and you put the phone on your nightstand. But wait, your cheap plastic phone case looks ridiculous on this titanium device. You need the leather case. That's $60. And then you realize your old wired headphones are incompatible. You need the AirPods Pro to really get the full experience. That's $250. Within 48 hours, that $1,200 purchase has quietly turned into a $1600 purchase, and you didn't even notice it happening. This isn't just you being bad with money. This is a psychological chain reaction that has destroyed more fortunes than the stock market ever could. It's a phenomenon that explains why winning the lottery often leads to bankruptcy and why buying a dream house can turn into a financial nightmare. It is called the Ditto effect. My name is Bobby and on this channel we explore the invisible scripts that keep us broke. Most people think they buy things because they need them. Today, I'm going to prove to you that you buy things because your other things are demanding them. If you want to stop the spiral and actually keep the money you earn, smash that like button and let's dive into the story of the man who lost everything because of a bathrobe. To understand why you can't stop spending money, we have to travel back to France in the year 1765. Meet Deni Dittoiro. He was a famous philosopher, the co-founder of the Encyclopedia and a brilliant mind. But despite his fame, Ditto was broke. He lived a humble life. He wore old clothes. He walked on old rugs. And he sat on a rickety wooden chair in a dusty library. And he was happy. He was content. But then everything changed. Catherine the Great, the Empress of Russia, heard about Ditto's financial struggles. She was a fan of his work, so she offered to buy his library from him for a massive sum of money, roughly the equivalent of $50,000 today, while letting him keep the books. Suddenly, Ditto was rich. So, what did he do? He did what any of us would do. He treated himself. He went out and bought a beautiful, expensive scarlet dressing gown, a luxury robe fit for a king. He brought it home, put it on, and looked in the mirror. He felt elegant. He felt wealthy. But as he sat down at his desk to write, he noticed something bothering him. The robe was magnificent, but his desk his desk was scratched, rotting, and covered in ink stains. The contrast was painful. The desk didn't match the elegance of the robe, so he replaced the desk. He bought a beautiful mahogany writing table. He sat down again. Now the robe and the desk looked great together. But as he looked down at the floor, he realized his old threadbear rug looked like a rag compared to the mahogany table. It was an insult to the room. So he brought a plush, expensive Damascus rug. You can guess what happened next. The rug made the curtains look cheap. He replaced the curtains. The curtains made the chair look like firewood. He bought a leather armchair. He bought new paintings, new sculptures, new mirrors. He spent months obsessing over the unity of his room. He systematically replaced every single object he owned until the entire environment matched the quality of the scarlet robe. And at the end of it, Dennis Ditto was broke again. He later wrote a famous essay titled Regrets on Parting with My Old Dressing Gown. In it, he wrote this haunting line. I was the absolute master of my old dressing gown, but I have become a slave to my new one. This is the Ditto effect. The introduction of a new possession into a consumer's existence will often result in a process of spiraling consumption. We think we own our things, but in reality, our things own us. Now, you might be thinking, "Okay, Bobby, that's a nice story about a French guy from 300 years ago, but I don't wear scarlet robes. How does this apply to me?" It applies to you every single day. The Ditto effect is actually more dangerous today than it was in 1765 because modern marketing is designed to trigger it. weaponized precision. Let's look at the fitness identity spiral. Let's say you decide to get in shape. You buy a Pelaton bike. That's a big purchase, maybe $1,500. You tell yourself, "This is an investment in my health. But when the bike arrives, you realize you can't ride it in your old baggy cotton t-shirt and gym shorts from high school. You don't look like the instructors on the screen. You don't feel like a cyclist. So, you buy the Specialized cycling shoes, $150. Then you buy the moisture wicking compression shorts, $80. Then you buy the branded tank top, $50. Then you realize the bike looks cluttered in your messy living room. You need to create a zen workout space. You buy a yoga mat, some dumbbells, maybe a new smart TV to cast the workouts. Suddenly, you haven't just bought a bike. You have bought an entire identity. This is the core psychology of the Ditto effect. Identity consistency. As humans, we crave consistency. We want our external world to match our internal self-image. When you buy a high status item like a luxury car or a designer handbag, you are upgrading your identity. If you view yourself as a Honda Civic person, you're comfortable wearing jeans and eating at McDonald's. But if you stretch your budget to buy a Porsche, you have shifted your identity. You are now a Porsche person. And Porsche people don't wear scratched sunglasses. Porsche people don't have cheap IKEA furniture. Porsche people don't eat off paper plates. The car acts as the anchor item. It sets a new baseline for your entire life. And every other item in your life that falls below that baseline creates psychological tension. It feels wrong. So to relieve that tension, you upgrade everything else. The car forces you to upgrade your wardrobe. The wardrobe forces you to upgrade your vacation spots. The vacation spots force you to upgrade your luggage. You aren't spending money because you want to. You are spending money to maintain coherence in your story. This is why the fake it till you make it advice is actually financially toxic. If you fake it by buying a Rolex before you can afford it, that Rolex is going to demand a suit, a car, and a dinner tab that will bankrupt you. Let's break down the math of the chain reaction cost. Most people calculate the cost of an item in isolation. They look at the price tag and say, "Can I afford this $500 item?" This is the wrong way to think. You need to calculate the chain reaction cost. Let's take the classic example, home renovation. You decide to renovate your kitchen. You budget $10,000 for new cabinets. That seems reasonable. But once the new white modern cabinets are installed, your yellowish 10-year-old refrigerator looks disgusting. It works perfectly fine, but visually it clashes. It breaks the consistency. So, you spend $2,000 on a stainless steel fridge. Now, the fridge and cabinets are sleek and modern, but looking down, your vinyl floor looks cheap and dated. The contrast is unbearable. So, you rip up the floor and put in hard wood. That's $5,000. Now, the kitchen is a masterpiece. It looks like a magazine cover, but it's an open concept house. So, when you stand in your beautiful new kitchen and look into the living room, the living room looks like a dump. The old brown sofa looks sad. The paint looks dull. The kitchen renovation has leaked into the living room. You end up painting the whole downstairs and buying a new sectional. The final cost, it wasn't $10,000. It was $35,000. The $10,000 cabinets were the scarlet robe. They were the anchor that made everything else look inadequate. If you had kept the old cabinets, you never would have noticed the floor. You never would have hated the fridge. You were happy with them before. The upgrade created the dissatisfaction. This brings us to a terrifying realization. Upgrades are often downgrades in disguise. When Ditto had his old robe, he didn't worry about ink stains. He used it to wipe his pen. It was functional. He was the master of it. When he got the new robe, he became terrified of ruining it. He became stiff. He lost his freedom. When you buy a new, brand new, expensive white couch, you stop letting your friends drink red wine in the living room. You stop letting the dog jump up. You stop living in your living room because you are servicing the object. You become the curator of a museum, not the resident of a home. So, how do we stop this? How do we break a psychological pattern that is hardwired into our brains? We can't just live in a cave and never buy anything nice. That's not realistic. But we can build firewalls to stop the spiral. Here is my three-step defense strategy against the Ditto effect. Strategy number one, predict the chain reaction. Before you buy any upgrade item, a new car, a new console, a new suit, you must pause and ask yourself, what else will this item demand? If you buy the PS5, will it demand a 4K TV to see the graphics properly? Will it demand an extra controller? Will it demand a subscription to PlayStation Plus? Write down the full system cost, not just the item cost. If the PS5 is $500, but the system cost is $1,500, can you afford the $1,500? If the answer is no, do not buy the anchor item. You are inviting a vampire into your house. Strategy number two, the buy one give one rule. The Dero effect thrives on accumulation. We add the new thing, but we keep the old things, and then we try to make the match. You need to cap your inventory. If you buy a new pair of sneakers, an old pair must leave the house. Donate it, sell it, or trash it. If you buy a new toaster, the old toaster goes. This forces you to value what you have. It prevents you from building a shrine of possessions. It keeps you in the mindset of a user, not a collector. Strategy number three, practice strategic downgrading. This is the nuclear option, but it works. Sometimes the only way to reset your baseline is to deliberately downgrade a visible part of your life. Drive a slightly older car than you can afford. Wear a watch that is simple and functional. When your anchor items are humble, you feel zero pressure to upgrade everything else. If you drive a beat up Toyota truck, nobody expects you to wear a $2,000 suit. You have freedom. You can wear jeans. You can eat a burrito in the car. By keeping your status symbols low, you lower the required cost of the rest of your life. You create a lowmaintenance identity. And let me tell you, a lowmaintenance identity is the most profitable asset you can own. It allows you to stack cash while everyone else is busy curating their museum. Look, there is nothing wrong with nice things. I like nice things. But you have to understand the game you are playing. Consumerism is designed to make you feel incomplete. It is designed to make you feel that you are just one purchase away from happiness. But Dero taught us the truth 300 years ago. That one purchase doesn't finish the puzzle. It scramles the puzzle. It resets the board and forces you to start over. Don't be a slave to your robe. Be the master of your life. - Stop Buying Stuff | Niko Stoifberg | TEDxBibliothekZug: Kind: captions Language: en Transcriber: Yuankai Gu Reviewer: David DeRuwe I would like to tell you a bit about an unusual New Year’s resolution that I made a couple of years ago. On New Year’s Eve 2015, I decided to stop buying stuff. Now, I hadn’t run out of money, and I wasn’t planning to spend a year in a cave meditating, and I also hadn’t any problems thinking about things that I would love to call my own. So what had happened to me? Well, what had happened was this: I had just come back from a holiday on Bali, which, you know, is being advertised as a paradise. But instead of pictures of gorgeous tropical nature, endless beaches and deep blue skies, the pictures that I remember that I still had in my mind were pictures of burning rubbish, of fire and smoke and heaps of plastic, and shorelines so deeply covered with waste that it was hard to tell where the beach was ending and where the ocean began. Both of them, the beach and the ocean, were covered beneath an endless blanket woven of all the thousands of colors that industrial materials can take, from the pink of brand new flip flops to the neon colors of children’s toys to the green and brown of plastic bottles. It was a huge wasteland of plastic, and I only saw the surface, the things that happened to stay afloat. Now, as I waded through this wasteland, I was both shocked and disgusted: shocked by the sheer amount of stuff and disgusted by the lifestyle that produced it - a lifestyle that happened to be my own. As a matter of fact, much of what washes up on the shores of Bali doesn’t actually have its origin on the island, but it finds its way there from every corner of the world where people can afford to throw it away. It was this holiday on Bali that made me want to stop buying stuff. Now, I’m no ascetic, I am not an activist, and I'm not against the market economy, but I couldn’t just turn away and pretend that I wasn’t responsible for this mess. I knew I was, and in fact, we all are. And it was back in Switzerland, a friend came visiting with three pairs of shoes that she had bought but never worn, and she was wondering whether maybe my girlfriend would like to try them on. Around the same time, another friend had just bought the new iPhone twice because he couldn't quite decide yet which screen size he preferred. And yet another friend was trading his car for the third time in three years. Crazy, but I myself, I wasn’t any better; I had just bought the same coat twice, once in olive green and once in a fancy color called “slate gray,” which wasn’t too different from olive green after all. So I couldn’t help but wonder, “Have we gone completely insane and was there a way to stop this madness?” What would happen if I just stopped it? I decided to give it a try. So for the next 12 months, I promised myself I wouldn’t buy anything. But I did allow myself two exceptions: Exception number one - I was still allowed to buy what I needed in order not to die. Rule number one, don't die. Exception number two - what I needed in order not to start stinking. That was rule number two, don’t stink. Or in other words, I was still allowed to buy food, which is rather helpful if you plan to do this for a year, and I was still allowed to buy things like soap, shampoo, toothpaste, etc. All the rest had to stay on the shelves. Now, was it difficult to do that? Was it difficult to do this with just these two exceptions? The surprising answer: “Not at all.” I quickly came up with two strategies that helped me avoid even the most attractive stuff: Strategy number one - instead of seeing offers as invitations, I started treating them as attacks, as personal attacks on me. So instead of saying, “Hey, look at this, this is great, I have to have this,” I tried to reframe the situation and say, “Wait a minute, they’re trying to trick me. They’re trying to sell me something that I don’t really need.” So every offer was, in fact, a trap, and my job was to to say, “No.” To not not fall into these traps: say no, no, no, and no again. That was strategy number one, and to put this strategy to a stress test, I decided to go to Zurich and walk down Bahnhofstrasse; you know, that street - it’s like a miracle mile of consumerism. And so I was walking down Bahnhofstrasse, and the first shop window that caught my attention was a sports gear vendor. They had skis in the window, and I love skiing. I love skiing more than almost everything else. So I saw those skis; they were awesome, but I also realized that they were exactly the same pair of skis that I already had at home, just in a different design. They just put on a different design every year. So I said, “No thanks,” and walked on. Next shop that I can remember was the Diesel store selling jeans. I was quite fond of that brand back then, so I looked at the jeans in the store, and I also began to wonder, “Did Lucky Luke?” - Are you familiar with Lucky Luke? My great childhood hero really is kind of - “Did Lucky Luke really own more than one pair of jeans?” And I don’t think he did. Next stop was the Apple store selling that new iPhone that my friend had bought twice, and about half the people I knew were already on it, on the latest version, and I was wondering whether I should be too. But then I asked myself, “Can this new phone really do anything that my old phone can’t, something that really matters?” and the obvious answer was no, so I said, “No thanks” and walked on Now, with this mindset, dishing out “nos” left and right, every little “no” started feeling like a victory. “You want to sell me this? No, thanks. Yes.” “You want to sell me that? So after a while of practicing, I was walking the streets in constant triumph, which felt good. And also, I realized that I suddenly had quite a bit of money left. Which brings me to strategy number two: When I felt like rewarding myself for my heroic persistence or to be honest, when I couldn’t fight the urge anymore to finally spend some of that money, I spent it on services instead of goods. So instead of buying a new t shirt, I decided to get a new haircut, or instead of buying a CD, which was still a thing back then, I decided to go to a concert. Instead of purchasing whatever happened to be “in,” I started to go out more often. Now, you could say, “OK, but this strategy number two, isn’t that just a cheap trick or a rather expensive trick?” Actually, I wasn’t really spending less; I was just spending it differently. And that’s true. But I can also assure you that this strategy number two, buying services instead of goods, doesn’t just work psychologically because it feels great to support your local services, it also works philosophically because as an economic activity, offering services is much, much more sustainable than the production of superfluous goods. Most services hardly produce any waste. And also, as an economic activity - it’s actually the economy that we all have to support if we want to decouple our growing prosperity, which we all want, from growing resource consumption, which is something that we should avoid. You could say that services are the economy of the future, if we choose to have one. And also, services foster social interaction. It makes a huge difference whether you sit at home and buy a new pair of shoes in front of your computer alone, or whether you go in to your local shoemaker, have your old boots repaired, and maybe have a chat with him or her. And last but not least, services do make us happier than goods. This may sound a little wishy-washy, but it’s actually well-proven scientific fact. The happiness we get from an experience, like a day on a mountain hiking, maybe using the service of a cable car, lasts much, much longer than the kick we get out of a material purchase, like that extra pair of hiking boots that you actually know you don’t really need. So you could say buying goods is like eating sugar, but experiences are much more nourishing for the soul. So after a year of buying nothing or almost nothing, I came to a conclusion that was both simple and surprising: buying less turns out to be a gain for yourself, for the environment, but also and even for the local economy. Now, did I eventually go back to buying stuff again? Yes, I did. It was the lack of socks that forced me to; I simply didn’t have any socks left that didn’t have any holes in them, and the situation started to get uncomfortable. But it also did provoke a new rule that I’ve been following ever since and that I would like to recommend to all of you. It goes like this: Whenever you buy something new, replace something old with it, and important, something old that is either used-up or broken, and if neither of those two things apply, then you don't buy the new thing. That's the rule. Following this new rule, I eventually had to give in and bought new socks, these very nice red ones that I’m still wearing today, which also taught me another lesson, maybe the most important one: Good things can last a very long time. Thank you. (Applause)

- Nobody Cares About Your WATCH: The Truth About Status: Kind: captions Language: en Why do you think the man with the Rolex on his wrist looks so nervous? You've seen him before. Maybe at the airport lounge, maybe at a conference, maybe in the lobby of a hotel you can't quite afford. He's checking his phone every 90 seconds. His leg bounces under the table. His eyes scan the room like a prey animal, waiting for something to strike. And on his wrist, catching the light just right, sits $20,000 worth of Swiss precision. But here's what nobody told you. That watch isn't making him feel powerful. It's making him feel trapped. Because somewhere deep in the architecture of his mind, he knows a secret that the entire luxury industry has spent a century trying to bury. Nobody cares. Not really. Not the way he needs them to. And the moment you understand why this is true, the moment you trace this lie back to its origin point in the wreckage of the Great Depression, everything about the world you live in starts to look different. This isn't a story about watches. This is a story about the most successful psychological operation ever run on the human species. And it started with a man who understood that the best way to sell someone a dream is to first convince them they're living in a nightmare. Let's go back. Let's go all the way back to when this whole machine was being built. Picture New York City in 1933. The depression has been grinding for 4 years now. Unemployment sits at 25%. Breadlines stretch around city blocks. Men in suits that used to mean something stand on street corners selling apples for a nickel. The stock market, which had promised to make everyone rich forever, has revealed itself to be exactly what it always was. A casino where the house always wins and the players always forget that the house always wins. But something else is happening in the shadows of this collapse. Something that will reshape how human beings understand their own worth for the next century. There's a man named Edward Bernay sitting in an office in Manhattan. He's Sigman Freud's nephew. He understands something about the human mind that makes him dangerous. He understands that people don't buy products because they need them. They buy products because they believe those products will transform who they are. And in 1933, in the ashes of the economy, he realizes that an entire generation of Americans is desperate for transformation. They've watched their fathers lose everything. They've seen the myth of the self-made man revealed as just that, a myth. And they're scared. Not just scared of poverty, scared of being nobody. Bernay doesn't invent advertising, but he invents something more powerful. He invents the idea that you can engineer desire that you can take a product any product and attach it to a deep human fear or longing and suddenly that product becomes necessary not useful necessary. He does this with cigarettes first. Convinces women that smoking is a form of liberation. Calls them torches of freedom. takes a health hazard and turns it into a political statement. And it works. It works so well that every corporation in America starts calling him and they all want the same thing. They want him to teach them how to make people feel incomplete because an incomplete person is a buying person. An incomplete person will keep reaching for the next thing and the next thing and the next thing trying to fill a hole that was deliberately carved into their psyche. Now, let's jump forward 20 years. It's 1953. The war is over. America won. The economy is booming. The suburbs are spreading across the country like a rash. And something new is happening. Something that would have been unthinkable during the depression. People have disposable income. Not just the rich, regular people, factory workers, salesmen, office clerks. They have money left over after paying for food and rent. And American industry, which spent the war years building tanks and bombers, suddenly has to figure out what to do with all these factories. The answer they come up with will define the next 70 years. They decide to build a culture of consumption to create an entire society based on the idea that buying things is not just pleasant. It's patriotic. It's your duty. It's how you prove you're a good American, a good person, a person who matters. This is where the watch comes in. Not as a tool, not as a way to tell time, but as a symbol, as a tiny machine you strap to your body that announces to the world that you have arrived, that you are successful, that you are worthy of being seen. The Swiss watch makers understand this immediately. They've been making watches for centuries, but now they're making something else. They're making tokens of achievement. They start advertising, not in technical magazines, but in lifestyle publications. In magazines that teach men how to dress, how to talk, how to impress a woman, how to get ahead at the office. The ads don't talk about craftsmanship or accuracy. They talk about success, about respect, about the look in another man's eyes when he notices what you're wearing. And it works because the underlying anxiety is real. The men buying these watches in the 1950s and60s are the sons and grandsons of the men who lost everything in the depression. They grew up watching their fathers scramble, watching them fail, watching them disappear into alcoholism or silence or rage. These men are terrified of ending up the same way. So when a magazine shows them a photograph of a confident man in a sharp suit with an expensive watch, they're not buying the watch. They're buying insurance against becoming their fathers. They're buying proof that they broke the cycle, that they made it out. But here's the trick that makes the whole system work. Here's the evil genius of it. The proof only works if other people see it. if other people validate it. You can't just feel successful in private. You need witnesses. You need the waiter to notice, the colleague to comment, the stranger at the bar to glance down at your wrist and make a calculation about who you are. The entire value of the status symbol depends on a collective agreement that this object means something. And that agreement has to be maintained constantly publicly or the whole thing falls apart. So now we arrive at the present day, at you, at me, at the man in the airport lounge with the Rolex and the bouncing leg. We've inherited this system. We were born into it. We've spent our entire lives breathing air that's been poisoned with the idea that objects can save us. That the right car, the right watch, the right shoes, the right anything will finally make us feel like we're enough. And most of us never question it. We just accept it as reality. We look at someone with an expensive watch and we think consciously or not, that person has made it. That person is winning. We want to be that person. But let me tell you what's actually happening in that person's head. Let me tell you what the research shows, what the psychologists have documented, what everyone in the luxury industry knows but will never admit publicly. The satisfaction is gone in 72 hours, sometimes less. You buy the watch, you feel incredible for about 3 days. You keep looking at it, turning your wrist to catch the light, imagining what people think when they see it. And then something happens. You get used to it. The watch becomes normal, becomes just another object on your body. And worse than that, much worse, you start noticing other watches, more expensive watches, rarer watches, watches that other people have that you don't, and the hunger comes back. The incompleteness returns. You're right back where you started, except now you're $20,000 poorer. This is called hedonic adaptation. It's the psychological principle that we return to a baseline level of happiness regardless of what happens to us. You can win the lottery and within a year you'll be exactly as happy or unhappy as you were before. You can buy the watch you've been dreaming about for 5 years and within a month it's invisible to you. Your brain is designed this way. It's designed to adapt, to normalize, to keep searching for the next thing that might give you an edge, might keep you alive, might make you matter to the tribe. This mechanism was useful when we were living in small groups on the African savannah. It kept us competitive, alert, hungry. But in a consumer economy, it's a trap because the economy needs you to stay hungry forever. It needs you to believe that satisfaction is always just one purchase away. That the next object will be the one that finally works. And the luxury industry knows this. They know it better than you do. They have department full of psychologists and market researchers whose entire job is to figure out how to keep you wanting, how to make sure that even after you buy the thing, you're already looking at the next thing. This is why watch companies release new models every year, limited editions, special collaborations, vintage reissues. It's not because the technology is improving. A mechanical watch from 1960 works exactly as well as a mechanical watch from today. It's because they need to create artificial scarcity, artificial urgency. They need you to believe that if you don't buy this particular model right now, you'll have missed something important, that you'll be left behind while other people move forward. Let me tell you about a study done in 2008. Researchers at Harvard looked at how people experience luxury purchases versus experiences. They found something fascinating. When people bought expensive objects, their happiness spiked immediately but returned to baseline within weeks. But when people spent money on experiences, travel, concerts, time with friends, their happiness increased and stayed elevated for months, sometimes years. Why? Because experiences become part of your identity. They change who you are. They give you stories, memories, perspectives. Objects just sit there. They're external. They can be lost, stolen, scratched, outdated. They don't integrate into the self. They remain separate, alien. No matter how much you paid for them. But here's what the researchers found that's even more disturbing. They discovered that people who base their self-worth on external validation, on the approval and admiration of others are significantly more likely to pursue status symbols. And they're also significantly more likely to report being anxious, depressed, and dissatisfied with their lives because they've built their sense of self on the most unstable foundation possible. Other people's opinions. and other people's opinions change constantly, shift randomly, depend on factors completely outside your control. You can have the perfect watch and walk into a room where everyone is wearing a PC Philippe and suddenly your Rolex looks cheap, looks desperate, and the shame you feel in that moment, that gut level sense of inadequacy, that's not an accident. That's the system working exactly as designed. So, who benefits from this system? Who profits when millions of people spend their lives chasing objects they don't need with money they don't have to impress people they don't like? The answer is obvious. The luxury brands, the financial institutions that loan you the money to buy their products, the marketing agencies that create the images and stories that make you want them in the first place. But there's a deeper answer, a more disturbing answer. The system itself benefits. The economic structure of modern capitalism requires constant growth. It requires that every quarter shows more revenue than the last quarter. More sales, more consumption, more extraction. And the only way to maintain that kind of growth indefinitely is to make sure people never feel satisfied, never feel complete, never feel like they have enough. This is why every advertisement you see is selling the same thing. It's not selling a product. It's selling the idea that you're currently inadequate and this product will fix you. You're not attractive enough, not successful enough, not respected enough, not young enough, not cool enough, not anything enough. But don't worry, we have the solution. Just buy this. Just $39.99. Just three easy payments. Just sign here and you'll be transformed. You'll be new. You'll be worthy. And the tragedy is that it works. Not because the products deliver on the promise. They never do. They can't. But because we want so desperately to believe. We want to believe there's a shortcut, a hack, a way to skip the hard work of actually becoming someone interesting, someone capable, someone at peace with themselves. We want to believe that we can purchase our way into maturity, into confidence. into meaning. And so we keep buying, keep hoping, keep telling ourselves that this time will be different, that this purchase will be the one that finally makes us feel whole. Let me tell you what nobody in the luxury industry will ever tell you. Let me give you the secret they've spent billions of dollars trying to hide. The people who are genuinely successful, genuinely confident, genuinely at peace with themselves, they don't care about your watch. They don't notice it. And if they do notice it, it doesn't change how they see you because they've learned something that most people never learn. They've learned that external validation is a drug that stops working. That the only opinion that matters is your own. and that you can't buy your way into self-respect. You can only earn it through the slow, difficult work of becoming someone you're proud to be. Think about the richest people in the world, the actual billionaires. What do they wear? Mark Zuckerberg wears a gray t-shirt every day. Warren Buffett lives in the same house he bought in 1958. Drives a car that's older than most people reading this. These people could afford to drape themselves in status symbols. They could wear a different watch every day for the rest of their lives. But they don't. Why? Because they've discovered something. They've discovered that once you have real power, real wealth, real security, you don't need to signal it. You don't need to prove anything to anyone. The compulsion to display status only exists when you're insecure about your status. when you're worried that people might not recognize how important you are. When you need constant reassurance that you matter. So, here's the question you need to ask yourself. Who are you performing for? When you buy the expensive watch, when you post the photo, when you angle your wrist just right in the meeting so people can see what you're wearing, who is that for? Is it for you really, or is it for the imagined audience in your head? Because whatever that fear is, whatever you think you're protecting yourself from by accumulating these objects, that fear is the real prison. Not your bank account, not your current situation. Your fear, your belief that without these external markers of success, you'll disappear. You'll become invisible. You'll be nobody. But let me offer you a different possibility. Let me suggest that the opposite is true. that the moment you stop performing, the moment you stop chasing validation, the moment you let go of the need to signal your worth to strangers, that's when you actually become somebody. That's when you become real. That's when you stop being a character playing a role and start being a person living a life. This doesn't mean you should live like a monk and reject all material comfort. It means you should understand why you're buying what you're buying. It means you should be honest with yourself about whether you actually want the object or whether you want the feeling you think the object will give you. And study two involved precisely that signaling test. They manipulated the visibility of the responses. If the costly signaling framework held true in this generalized setting, the public group should have agreed more strongly with the luxury belief statements than the private group did. >> And the result was null. >> The result was null. There was no statistical evidence that participants signal status through luxury beliefs when their responses were shown to an audience versus kept private. So that motive to signal was weak or maybe even non-existent in this close to anonymous general population setup. And this finding remained robust even when they controlled for all sorts of demographic variables. >> So what does this failure to find an active signaling motive in the general population imply about how these ideas are spreading? Well, it confirms that these ideas have not yet spread outside the specific highly validated social networks, the particular university campuses, activist groups or professional intellectual circles where a specific small audience validates them as high status signals. For the broader public, the signal is just too noisy or the payoff for adopting these beliefs as a social signal is currently insufficient to motivate dishonest signaling. The study doesn't debunk the concept of luxury beliefs. But that highly localized dialect is about to hit a massive accelerator when it enters the digital realm. >> Right? The underlying human motive for status is constant. We've moved from ptox to top hats to abstract philosophical beliefs. But social media takes that fundamental ancient need for status and just optimizes the reward system. It replaces the organic slow feedback loop of a village or a university with manufactured hypereefficient incentives. >> This is where we need to apply costly signaling theory not to the beliefs but to the infrastructure itself. Platforms introduce powerful explicit rewards, likes, retweets, follower counts through what's formerly called gamification. And these are non-epistic incentives. They have nothing to do with the truthfulness or the reliability of the information being shared. That's the core mechanism that just warps the entire goal of conversation. Instead of the goal being communication or truth, you know, epistemic goals, the system incentivizes users to chase quantifiable metrics. This fundamentally alters the payoff structure. It reduces the cost of sharing false or inflammatory content because the potential status reward often overwhelms any reputational costs associated with being wrong. And the architecture is intentionally uh behaviorally engineered. These platforms aren't designed for rational agents. They are designed based on the psychological knowledge that users are emotional, reactive, and driven by cognitive shortcuts. They leverage our biases for maximum engagement. >> Let's look at how that engineering plays out. For example, the use of variable rewards. >> This is straight out of BF Skinner's work on intermittent reinforcement. It mimics the mechanism of a slot machine platforms like Instagram and Twitter. They vary the timing, the source, and the intensity of likes, comments, or followers. >> So, you don't know when the reward is coming. >> You don't. You might get three likes instantly or 50 likes 6 hours later. This unpredictability heightens the dopamine response and creates an addictive loop. You are trained to constantly check back, chasing that high status signal. >> They also engineer urgency using loss aversion, capitalizing on our tendency to fear losing something more than we value gaining something equivalent. Exactly. Features like disappearing content or those social media streaks, they create urgency. You have to view it before it's gone or you trigger emotional dissonance if the engagement pattern is broken. It creates a reliance on the platform to maintain your social connections which makes disengaging feel costly. >> Then there's choice architecture which is designed to minimize cognitive load and maximize effortless consumption. Like how YouTube autoplay defaults to playing the next video or how Facebook prioritizes comments based on most relevant. Yeah, autoplay removes the friction of having to choose the next video, which makes consumption effortless and often leads users down these algorithmic rabbit holes. Sorting comments by most relevant subtly guides users to align with the platforms or the algorithm's preferred bias, reducing the likelihood they'll seek out diverse or critical viewpoints, which would involve more cognitive effort. >> And this architecture doesn't just manage behavior. It specifically makes misinformation and subsequently the spread of luxury beliefs cheaper and easier to propagate. The key new tool for this cheap signaling is the act of reposting, sharing, retweeting, forwarding. Reposting is the quintessential cheap signal. It requires virtually zero cognitive production effort. It's instantaneous. You get the benefit of broadcasting an idea, claiming the status or moral sophistication that comes with it without incurring any of the material or cognitive production effort required to actually articulate the idea yourself. >> It violates a fundamental tenant of costly signaling theory. >> It does. If the cost of producing the signal is negligible, the system becomes unstable. And this negligible cost leads directly to a massive reduction in reputational risk through plausible deniability. A repost is inherently ambiguous. >> And that ambiguity is the magic ingredient. Does the user fully endorse the content? Are they just sharing it as a point of interest or for discussion? Because that intention is unclear, the ambiguity dramatically reduces the reputational risks. The sender always retains the option to immediately disown authorship and responsibility if the content turns out to be false or problematic or if the social consensus shifts against it. >> So the platform provides a built-in mechanism for insincere signaling. It wasn't my original thought. >> Exactly. The ability to consistently, if insincerely, deny the problematic interpretation makes reposting a highly convenient vehicle for lowcost risky communication. While these cheaper signals are generally less persuasive than a confident direct assertion, the minimal reputational cost coupled with the immense digital reach makes it the dominant form of status interaction online. And this is why we're starting to see platform design interventions trying to combat these behavioral shortcuts by increasing the cost of signaling. Things like making quote tweets the default for sharing or prompting users to read a link before they share it. >> Those are explicit counter nudges. They're aimed at reintroducing friction into the system. From a CST perspective, they're trying to artificially increase the production cost of the signal. They force a momentary pause, engaging the more reflective system of human thought and reminding the user of the reputational stakes involved before an instantaneous emotionally driven repost occurs. But even beyond the manipulation of friction, the core problem of the digital environment is that it fundamentally degrades the monitoring that's necessary for costly signaling to maintain honest communication. If violations of truthfulness aren't easily detected and sanctioned, the entire reputational infrastructure just collapses because deception becomes cheap. >> And the single biggest factor hindering that detection is the sheer magnitude of information, what we call information overload. The numbers are just staggering. The volume of data circulating globally is now estimated to be around 120 zetytes annually. And that number is escalating rapidly. Our cognitive resources, however, are finite. Our epistemic vigilance, that active mental defense system we have to guard against deception. It just gets overloaded. >> It's completely overwhelmed. We can't effectively monitor every source, fcheck every claim, or verify every piece of content. The practical consequence for the person spreading misinformation is a direct reduction in cost. Secondly, Control What&nbsp; You Can, Camp introduces the concept of focusing&nbsp;&nbsp; on elements within the negotiator's control.&nbsp; This strategy involves careful preparation,&nbsp;&nbsp; defining clear goals, and understanding one's own&nbsp; boundaries and limits. By focusing on what can be&nbsp;&nbsp; controlled, such as one's attitude, preparation&nbsp; level, and how they present their arguments,&nbsp;&nbsp; negotiators can avoid feeling helpless&nbsp; or reactive to the other party's demands.&nbsp;&nbsp; This emphasis on control helps in maintaining&nbsp; discipline throughout the negotiation process,&nbsp;&nbsp; ensuring that decisions are made based on&nbsp; strategy rather than emotion. It also encourages&nbsp;&nbsp; negotiators to remain flexible and adaptive,&nbsp; adjusting their approaches based on the situation&nbsp;&nbsp; while maintaining a clear sense of direction&nbsp; towards their ultimate goal.Thirdly, Building a&nbsp;&nbsp; Vision, Jim Camp advocates for the importance of&nbsp; building a vision of the desired outcome as part&nbsp;&nbsp; of the negotiation process. This involves not only&nbsp; having a clear sense of what one wants to achieve&nbsp;&nbsp; but also understanding the needs and goals of the&nbsp; other party. By developing a comprehensive view of&nbsp;&nbsp; the possible outcomes, negotiators can steer the&nbsp; conversation towards solutions that are mutually&nbsp;&nbsp; beneficial, even if the negotiation started with a&nbsp; 'no.' This foresight enables negotiators to guide&nbsp;&nbsp; discussions with purpose and direction, creating&nbsp; a framework within which creative and satisfactory&nbsp;&nbsp; solutions can be discovered. Building a vision&nbsp; helps in turning adversarial negotiations into&nbsp;&nbsp; collaborative problem-solving sessions, where&nbsp; both parties are invested in finding the best&nbsp;&nbsp; outcome.Fourthly, The Importance of Listening, One&nbsp; of the critical tools in Jim Camp's negotiation&nbsp;&nbsp; strategy is the skill of active listening.&nbsp; By truly listening to the other party—paying&nbsp;&nbsp; attention not just to what is said, but also&nbsp; to what is left unsaid—negotiators can gain&nbsp;&nbsp; valuable insights into the other party's true&nbsp; priorities and constraints. This understanding&nbsp;&nbsp; can then be used to craft proposals that address&nbsp; those needs while still advancing one's own goals.&nbsp;&nbsp; Camp emphasizes that effective listening can&nbsp; transform negotiations by building trust and&nbsp;&nbsp; openness, facilitating a more in-depth exploration&nbsp; of potential solutions. It requires patience,&nbsp;&nbsp; empathy, and a genuine willingness to understand&nbsp; the other party's perspective, making it a&nbsp;&nbsp; powerful tool for achieving favorable negotiation&nbsp; outcomes. Lastly, Disciplined Preparation,&nbsp;&nbsp; At the core of Camp's negotiation philosophy is&nbsp; the principle of disciplined preparation. This&nbsp;&nbsp; means entering negotiations with a well-researched&nbsp; understanding of the other party's position,&nbsp;&nbsp; potential objections, and the broader context&nbsp; in which the negotiation takes place. Such&nbsp;&nbsp; preparation involves crafting precise questions&nbsp; to uncover information, setting clear objectives&nbsp;&nbsp; for the negotiation, and developing a nuanced&nbsp; strategy that anticipates various negotiation&nbsp;&nbsp; dynamics. - Influence & Persuasion: Crash Course Media Literacy #6: Kind: captions Language: en Let’s play a little game of “name that tune.” I’m going to start singing a tune, and I want you see if you can finish it without me. Ok here it goes: “Ba da ba ba ba…” What about, “I am stuck on Band Aid Brand....” Did you hear that in the little kids’ voice? That’s a cute one. OK last one: “Gimme a break, gimme a break.” C’mon you had to know that one. If you didn’t finish at least one of those on your own, I’d be shocked. These little songs advertisers use in commercials are called jingles, and you know these popular ones because they were written specifically to get stuck in your head. Catchy tunes are just one technique advertisers use to get you to remember them and, hopefully, buy their stuff. For years psychologists and sociologists have studied why humans buy things, and brands use that research to hack our brains and open our wallets. By applying the skills we’ve learned so far, we can protect ourselves from buying yet another fancy frappuccino off the not-so-secret secret menu. Today we’re going to un-hack your brain on advertising. [Theme Music] First things first: let’s define advertising and its close cousins, public relations and propaganda. An advertisement is a public notice promoting a product, event, or service. Advertising is the art of creating those. Sometimes brands create ads themselves, and sometimes they hire companies to do it for them. Yes, just like the people from Mad Men. Public relations, or PR, is something different. PR is the management of the relationship between the public (that’s you) and a brand. PR tells the public what the brand is up to and tries to make the brand look as good as possible. They’re the people who write the apology when someone makes a mistake or build the hype around the latest iPhone release. Finally, propaganda is information distributed with the direct purpose of promoting a certain point of view. This info is often misleading or biased, and propaganda is usually used to promote specific political viewpoints. These definitions may seem tidy, but the differences between these fields can be really hard to distinguish out in the real world, especially online. Don’t worry, we’ll talk a lot more about propaganda later in the course. Last time on Crash Course Media Literacy, we learned that all media is constructed. Creators make choices each step of the way, from their work’s purpose and focus to the point of view they use to tell their story. Advertisements work the same way, from the split-second ad you swipe through before watching your friends’ stories to elaborate movie trailers that get as much hype as the movie itself. On top of that, ads are created using a century’s worth of market research: experiments carried out to discover what makes us want to buy things. Advertisers use that knowledge to tap into our desires, often exploiting our most basic needs – not only the food and shelter kind, but the love and belonging kind, too. One of the pioneers of this somewhat sinister art was Edward Bernays. Working in the 1920s and ‘30s, he wrote: “The human being—male or female—is a herd animal. Man is fearful of solitude...He is more sensitive to the voice of the herd than to any other influence.” That’s from his 1923 book Crystallizing Public Opinion, which became a classic in the public relations field. It detailed how humans can be persuaded to change their habits if it will help them to follow the crowd. Think back to middle school. What was that one trend that everyone had to follow, or you totally felt left out? Friendship bracelets, the latest pair of Jordans, a fidget spinner, one of those little electronic keychain pets – seriously what was the deal with those things? Chances are you or your friends bought them because everyone else had one – you wanted to fit in. Advertisements love to play on this need, and that’s how trends and fads happen in the first place. In the 1940’s, psychologist Abraham Maslow added another piece to this puzzle. He identified a hierarchy of needs he said all humans had. It’s set up like a pyramid. At the base, the foundation, all humans need food and water, shelter, and sleep. Just above that, they need to feel safe, too. Then comes the need for love and feeling like you belong somewhere. After that, we need to feel accomplished, like we matter. At the tippy top of the pyramid is the need to fulfill our destiny, to be our best selves. Now all of these needs, combined with our natural desire to follow the crowd, are like little buttons on our hearts and brains. Advertisements press different combinations of buttons in hopes that we’ll respond the right way. Usually that means buying their product. The sales pitch of most modern ads is that product X will satisfy your need for Y. For example, security systems promise one of our most basic instincts: safety. We want to be safe, so we buy alarms to keep out the bad guys. And Slim Jims? They promise food – of a sort. Down at the bottom of the pyramid. But some products claim to satisfy multiple needs higher up on that pyramid. Let’s head into the Thought Bubble to take a closer look. Check out this vintage ad for hair dye. It features L’Oreal’s iconic slogan “Because you’re worth it.” They’ve used this slogan more or less since 1971. In this ad, it’s used with the claim that this dye is the most expensive in the country. Usually, that’s not a great way to sell a lot of anything. But the slogan “because you’re worth it” presses a lot of our human need buttons. For starters, any advertisement for hair dye implies that natural hair color is boring. So, for other people to like us, to stick with the herd, our hair has to be a different, better color. But still a pretty normal, human-y color, so we don’t stick out from the herd. That’s the button for feeling loved and like we belong. But there’s also that need for accomplishment, like we matter. We’re worth it. The ad is saying, you’re hot. You’re the best. You deserve this product. You deserve the most expensive dye, even though it’s luxury. Nay, BECAUSE it’s luxury. Not only is this ad an appeal to stick with the herd, to blend in with beauty norms, but it’s also an appeal to individualism. It’s an appeal to that middle of the pyramid and the tippy top, the desire to become our best selves and rise above the rest of the herd. It’s genius, really. If you’ve ever screamed TREAT YOSELF while splurging on a pair of designer shoes after a long day, you’ve fallen into this ad trap. Thanks for the help, Thought Bubble. Once an advertiser knows which “need button” to press, they need to persuade you that it will work. Turns out that there are a few things that really persuade us. The first is authority: if we think the person talking is an expert, we’re likely to believe them. Like in those “5 out of 5 dentists recommend” toothpaste commercials. Dentists know teeth, right? The next is likeability: if we like them, are friends with them, or trust them, we’re also likely to listen. That's why brands use extremely popular and respected celebrities, like, say, Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet, to sell watches or perfume. Same with consistency: if what’s being said vibes with what we already believe, we’ll probably go along with it. If everything you’ve ever heard about this new true crime podcast says its great and thrilling and awesome, you probably wouldn’t believe your coworker’s negative review of it. If there’s a consensus around something, if it’s popular, we are easily swayed to think it’s good, too. And if we think it’s a scarce resource and we could have a piece of it, it’s even more attractive. So, if everyone else had an iPhone and you didn’t, you’d probably really want one. And if a limited edition version came out that was signed by Beyonce you’d want that one even more. Advertisers often use these persuasive qualities in benign ways to get us to buy one brand of chocolate over another or something. But they can also be used against us by being baked into false claims. They’re not lying, exactly, but making claims based on poor or misleading logic. One popular type of fallacy in advertising is an appeal to emotions. This is when an ad convinces you to take action by tugging at your heartstrings. Those sad sick dog commercials with the Sarah McLachlan song? That’s an appeal to emotions. Just because sick dogs make you sad doesn’t automatically mean an organization deserves a donation; it just makes you link the two together. (I mean, please still save the sick dogs, this is just an example folks.) Then there’s the false dilemma, where an ad shows you a limited number of choices so you won’t consider all of the options. Laundry detergent ads for example, seem to always go “head to head” with another brand – but only one other brand, even though there are dozens. Another popular one is the red herring, the presentation of something totally irrelevant to distract you from the issue at hand. This happens in politics all the time. Ever seen a TV campaign ad during a local election that shouted something totally unrelated at you? Like, “Don’t elect Dan, his daughter eats CEREAL!” And suddenly you’re wondering what’s wrong with cereal until you forget that cereal has nothing to do with politics. Then there’s traditional wisdom, the idea that you should pick something because that’s how your grandmom or your old man used to do it. But your old man used a record player because there wasn’t any other option, not because he wanted to lug around a crate full of vinyl to every single party. All of these fallacies and persuasive techniques can be used for good and for evil and in between. Public service campaigns can get kids to stop smoking or invest in local journalism. But on the other hand, cosmetics ads can harm teens’ body images, causing eating disorders and depression. The better psychologists and sociologists get at persuading the human brain – even if their intentions are good – the better bad actors get at it, too. All the more reason to stretch your media literacy muscles. Today we talked about how advertisements can make you change your mind. Next time on Crash Course Media Literacy we’re going to tell you when and where they’re doing it. We’re going to talk all about those creepy targeted ads that follow you around the internet and much, much more. See you next time. Until then, I’m Jay Smooth. - How Ads (and People) Persuade You: Kind: captions Language: en [♪♩INTRO] Every day, you are bombarded with ads, salespeople, or friends trying to persuade you to do something, like watch a new show on Netflix or try out a new diet. Those messages don’t always convince you, but sometimes they do — and you might not even realize it’s happening. Dozens of factors can cause you to agree or disagree with a message, and a lot of them have to do with how you respond to persuasion in the first place. But if you can recognize when you’re being persuaded, it’s a lot easier to stop and make sure your opinions are actually your own. A lot of researchers who study persuasion think about it in terms of what’s called the Elaboration Likelihood Model, or ELM, which divides your response to persuasion into two main categories: There’s the central route, where you thoughtfully consider a message, or the peripheral route, where you make a decision using quick judgements or gut feelings. Most of the time, you end up using the peripheral route — like when you’re watching a commercial and decide the actor playing a doctor knows what she’s talking about because she’s wearing a white coat. Obviously, it’s good to think critically about some things, but we don’t have time to do that for everything, so both routes are important and useful. It helps to recognize which route you’re taking, though, so you can decide whether it’s worth stopping to think critically about whatever someone’s trying to convince you of. A few things can affect which route you take. Some are personality traits, like what’s known as the need for cognition, which describes how much people like to think about things. People with a higher need for cognition tend to pay close attention to arguments, while people with a low need prefer to make decisions based on quick cues, like how credible someone seems. One experiment in 1986 showed that people with a high need are more likely to take the central route, while those with a low need tend to take the peripheral route. In the study, researchers presented a few hundred university students with strong and weak arguments for raising the school’s tuition. They found that strong arguments were more persuasive than weak ones, but especially when students had a high need for cognition. You’ll also be more likely to use the central route if a topic is important to you. If you’re obsessed with good TV and someone says they’ve found the best show ever, you might spend hours looking at its cinematography and writing before you decide you agree with them. But if you just want something to binge watch, you might not care about all that. If a TV-loving friend says Game of Thrones is the best thing they’ve ever seen, that might be enough to convince you… especially if you hear it over and over and over again, every Sunday night. I gave up. I finally watched Game of Thrones. Are you happy? The situation is also important. Even if you love the topic, you’re more likely to use the peripheral route if you’re distracted or don’t have much time to think. Other factors are less straightforward, which is where persuasion gets complicated. For example, feeling an emotion can persuade you in a bunch of different ways depending on the situation. An emotion could be critical evidence, like if you’re trying to figure out if a comedy movie is good. If you felt happy while watching it, that’s a pretty good reason to decide that you liked it. Other times, your emotions can influence your opinions without you actively thinking about If you feel good watching a commercial, for example, you’ll probably feel good about the product, too. Emotions can also affect how you think and how much you think about something. If you’re in a positive mood, you might not think as deeply about what you’re hearing. So the same emotion can persuade you in different ways, depending on the context. But they can also make you more vulnerable to being convinced of something without thinking critically about it. The credibility and source of the message also play a big part. A 2016 study found that people who read a product review were more likely to think negatively about the product if they knew the review was sponsored. That’s probably because, if we know someone was paid to say good things, it’s harder for us to trust that the message is true, so we’ll think more critically about it. We’re also more likely to think harder about arguments if the message comes from someone in the minority opinion. In an experiment in Spain, students read a message that supported making green the official school color. When the message said the majority of students supported the idea, it didn’t much matter whether the arguments for it were good or bad. The reader already thought it was probably a good idea. But if it was a minority opinion, they only tended to think it was a good idea if it had good arguments. Meaning that if you see lots of people sharing something on Facebook, for example, you might not think as critically about whether the content itself is actually making a good point. But if only one friend shares that opinion, the argument starts to matter more. So, there are a lot of different things that can affect whether a commercial or person will persuade you. None of them are guaranteed to work, though — especially if you realize what’s happening. Your mind is your own, and when you recognize that you’re in a situation where you’re more likely to be convinced of something, you can decide whether it’s worth taking a little bit of time to think about it. Thanks for watching this episode of SciShow Psych! If you’d like to see more videos like this about the complicated things that make our brains and minds work, you can go to youtube.com/scishowpsych and subscribe.
