But we do make a lot of&nbsp;&nbsp; our decisions subconsciously. And that's&nbsp; where neuromarketing comes in. Companies&nbsp;&nbsp; are trying to better understand how our brain&nbsp; works – to figure out what we really want.&nbsp; "Traditional marketing studies work like this.&nbsp; Someone will ask me: do you want an apple&nbsp;&nbsp; or do you want a chocolate bar? And I'd&nbsp; say: I of course want the apple.&nbsp;&nbsp; But… do I really want the apple?” "We feel as if we're in control, we feel as&nbsp;&nbsp; if we're the author of our decisions and we're&nbsp; thinking through these things very rationally.&nbsp;&nbsp; But study after study after study shows that&nbsp; we are extremely irrational and that we're,&nbsp;&nbsp; generally speaking, pretty unaware of the&nbsp; full range of factors which ultimately&nbsp;&nbsp; inform and sometimes actually decide the&nbsp; different behaviors and paths that we take."&nbsp; "In short: we don't always know what we&nbsp; want. We don't know if we actually want the&nbsp;&nbsp; apple or if we prefer the chocolate&nbsp; bar. But our brain doesn't lie." &nbsp; And that's why neuromarketers have adopted a range&nbsp; of technologies in their marketing studies to see&nbsp;&nbsp; what's happening under the hood--inside consumers'&nbsp; brains. Functional magnetic resonance imaging&nbsp;&nbsp; and electroencephalograms measure activity&nbsp; in the brain. Eye-tracking shows where we&nbsp;&nbsp; direct our attention. Heart rate and skin&nbsp; conductance show what we find exciting.&nbsp; "For better or worse, people are complex&nbsp; and the brain is really complex." &nbsp; Uma Karmarkar is a scholar whose research&nbsp; revolves around how we make decisions. &nbsp; "What neuroscience does is it gives us&nbsp; access to some of these emotional elements or&nbsp;&nbsp; these elements that might not be fully conscious&nbsp; and tells us a little bit more about some of the&nbsp;&nbsp; things that might also be contributing&nbsp; to people's experiences and choices." &nbsp; "Take Cheetos, for example. When its parent&nbsp; company Frito-Lay asked consumers how they felt&nbsp;&nbsp; about the brand, many said: well, it's a bit of a&nbsp; kids' snack. But when they looked at their brains,&nbsp;&nbsp; it turned out people got a real kick out of&nbsp; getting their fingers messy with this orange&nbsp;&nbsp; dust that they're covered in. It IS fun…" "There was something subversive about that&nbsp;&nbsp; orange dust on your fingers. There was&nbsp; something a little unusual about it,&nbsp;&nbsp; and people kind of enjoyed it, even&nbsp; though it was not that respectable." &nbsp; Frito-Lay took these findings and built an&nbsp; entire ad campaign around this feeling of&nbsp;&nbsp; subversive pleasure. It became a huge success.&nbsp; "More and more businesses are investing&nbsp; in this type of research – most of&nbsp;&nbsp; which is happening in secret." Through neuroscience – but&nbsp;&nbsp; also with the help of psychology and behavioral&nbsp; economics – they get a pretty good idea of what&nbsp;&nbsp; makes us tick. And they use this knowledge&nbsp; to get us to buy more of their stuff. &nbsp; "I'm going to give you four examples of this that&nbsp; you've probably seen in your everyday life." &nbsp; One: They wear you down. Our brain operates in two different&nbsp;&nbsp; thinking modes. There's what's called system&nbsp;1, which is fast, unconscious and automatic. And then there's system 2, which is deliberate&nbsp; and conscious – but takes a LOT of effort.&nbsp; "If I ask you: what is your name? System&nbsp;1 will immediately have an answer to that&nbsp;question. But if I ask you what is 23 times&nbsp;48, you're going to have to switch to system&nbsp;2. This requires effort. Now imagine,&nbsp; you're going grocery shopping." &nbsp; You have to find your way around the&nbsp; different aisles and make loads of decisions&nbsp;&nbsp; in a short amount of time. When you finally&nbsp; get to the checkout counter, you're tired. &nbsp; "One way in which you can get somebody to be more&nbsp;system 1 oriented is actually through wearing them&nbsp;down. So system 2, very resource intensive,&nbsp;&nbsp; requires a lot of metabolic resources.&nbsp; When we're tired, when we're malnourished,&nbsp;&nbsp; we're much more likely to go with a much&nbsp; more impulsive system 1 response." And that's why right at the end of your&nbsp; shopping trip, retailers tempt you with&nbsp;&nbsp; loads and loads of sugary snacks – that you&nbsp; might just pick up at the very last moment. &nbsp; Shopping malls exploit the same situation.&nbsp; They're confusing, they're overwhelming, they're&nbsp;&nbsp; quite frankly exhausting – so you're more prone to&nbsp; spend money on something you might not even need. &nbsp; Two: They tell you what the right price is. "Let's say you walk into a store and see&nbsp;&nbsp; a bottle of wine for, I don't know, let's say 15&nbsp;&nbsp;dollars. Your brain doesn't really know&nbsp; if this a lot or this is not a lot. &nbsp; So, it's&nbsp;immediately starting to look for some context." "Typically, people don't really have a sense of&nbsp;&nbsp;price, like they don't really know how much wine&nbsp; should cost or what's the right price of a wine."&nbsp; This is Moran Cerf, a computer hacker turned&nbsp; neuroscientist and business professor.&nbsp; "People create their kind of impressions&nbsp; of the price range not by knowledge, by information – but by sampling reality." The store will happily give your brain&nbsp;a reality to latch onto – by placing a&nbsp;second bottle next to it, costing 50$.&nbsp;&nbsp; Now your brain thinks: 15$, that's&nbsp; actually a PRETTY good deal. So it's&nbsp;&nbsp; very likely you're going to buy this bottle. "Our brains are like ships, we're looking&nbsp;&nbsp; for places to anchor, right? And adding any&nbsp; sort of context or understanding of value,&nbsp;&nbsp; having an anchor helps." Three: They keep you on the treadmill. &nbsp; Another quirk of our brain that brands&nbsp;are using is that it's constantly seeking&nbsp;pleasure. And the key word here is "seeking". "Once you're experiencing a sort of thing that&nbsp;you wanted, you don't just get to bask in that&nbsp;pure pleasure for a long time. It's not the type&nbsp; of emotion which is enduring over time. And&nbsp; that's a very, very good thing for brands." &nbsp; Because pleasure is so fleeting, brands&nbsp;keep sending us to what's called the&nbsp;"hedonic treadmill". "…the iPhone 6…" &nbsp; "…the iPhone 6S…" "…this is iPhone 7…"&nbsp; "…iPhone 11…" "…the iPhone 12…" "You buy an iPhone 8. It's a brand new physical&nbsp; design and you're loving it. And just like&nbsp;&nbsp; clockwork, 12 months later, 8S comes out. Whatever&nbsp; pleasure you got from achieving and purchasing&nbsp;&nbsp; the iPhone is now immediately gone. And now&nbsp; you're looking to again, jump on the hedonic&nbsp;&nbsp; treadmill and look, chase the next pleasure." Four: They hide little nudges in plain sight. &nbsp; "So… you remember that cinema&nbsp; story from the beginning?&nbsp;&nbsp; Subliminal marketing messages like this, so&nbsp; things that we can't pick up on consciously,&nbsp;&nbsp; are actually illegal in most countries. But a&nbsp; few companies must have thought: well, why don't&nbsp;&nbsp; we just hide them in plain sight?" Check out this ad from KFC. See anything unusual?&nbsp;&nbsp; Well, look again. There's an actual&nbsp; dollar bill photoshopped into the&nbsp;&nbsp; burger – which happens to cost 1 dollar. And check out this can. Coca-Cola made it&nbsp;&nbsp; look like it's smiling-- to tie in&nbsp; with its brand image of happiness. &nbsp; And in literally every ad for watches, the time&nbsp; is set to 10 past 10. Because that makes it&nbsp;look like the watch is smiling at you. These&nbsp;types of subtle hints are called 'primers'. &nbsp; "I would say right now, it's controversial whether&nbsp; priming works. That said, we still teach that in&nbsp;&nbsp; school and in business school as kind of a&nbsp; mechanism people should be aware of because&nbsp;&nbsp; it's easy to implement. For the small&nbsp; chance that it does work, why not try it,&nbsp;&nbsp; if you're trying to sell something" "If you see a 10:10 watch, you're not compelled&nbsp;&nbsp; by some physical force to go out and do everything&nbsp; you can to buy it. But if you're already feeling&nbsp;&nbsp; like buying a watch, maybe you're very favorable&nbsp; towards the brand, and that additional data point&nbsp;&nbsp; is going to push you maybe a little bit further." And this is not limited to visual triggers.&nbsp;&nbsp; An experiment showed that if a&nbsp; wine store plays French music,&nbsp;&nbsp; customers buy more French wine. And if it&nbsp; plays German music, they buy more German wine. &nbsp; "A lot of this stuff is hiding in archives for&nbsp; companies and it is in their best interest not&nbsp;&nbsp; to reveal it. But we would be silly to think&nbsp; that this isn't part of the experiential&nbsp;&nbsp; design that companies are creating to&nbsp; better engage with their consumers." &nbsp; So where does all this leave us? Are&nbsp; we ultimately just puppets, without a will&nbsp;&nbsp; of our own, buying whatever corporations&nbsp; throw our way? Or do we have a choice? &nbsp; "Totally mindless behavior is rare, total&nbsp; control is also rare. And in between there's a&nbsp;&nbsp; wide gray area and we can move the&nbsp; needle between whether we make choices&nbsp;&nbsp; that are very informed and very kind of thorough.&nbsp; Or very impulsive and not too thorough." \&nbsp; "If you like something that's going to be&nbsp; the most important determinant of whether&nbsp;&nbsp; or not you choose to spend money on it or your&nbsp; time on it or your resources in general on it.&nbsp;&nbsp; And that speaks a lot to the power that&nbsp; we have as consumers and individuals." "Now, neuromarketing is a very powerful tool.&nbsp; It gives companies access to something that&nbsp;&nbsp; even we don't even have access to: our&nbsp; subconscious. But just knowing that and&nbsp;&nbsp; knowing how our brain works, can&nbsp; already help us make better decisions."&nbsp; Have you ever come across any of the things&nbsp; we've shown you in the video? Let us know... What was...what was that? … did you see that? Anyway. Let&nbsp;us know in the comments. And hit subscribe&nbsp;for more videos like this every Friday.

- Neuromarketing: 15 Neuromarketing Examples: Kind: captions Language: en ﻿Neuromarketing is taking over the world, and&nbsp; almost every big business and university has used&nbsp;&nbsp; it in some way. Even though neuromarketing&nbsp; is so important in the marketing world,&nbsp;&nbsp; many people don't know what it is or how it can&nbsp; be used successfully. The next 15 interesting&nbsp;&nbsp; examples of neuromarketing in work are shown&nbsp; in the animations below. 1. Why eye gaze is&nbsp;&nbsp; important 106 It's no secret that ads with people&nbsp; in them work much better than those without.&nbsp;&nbsp; In particular, people tend to look at pictures&nbsp; and movies with babies for longer and pay more&nbsp;&nbsp; attention to them. Advertisers have tried for&nbsp; a long time to sell more baby goods by showing&nbsp;&nbsp; close-ups of cute baby faces, but eye tracking&nbsp; technology has shown that this is not enough.&nbsp;&nbsp; Researchers found that when the baby looks&nbsp; straight at the camera, people pay much more&nbsp;&nbsp; attention to the baby's face and less attention&nbsp; to what the ad is about. But if the baby is&nbsp;&nbsp; looking at the object or text, the viewer will&nbsp; actually pay attention to what the ad is about.&nbsp;&nbsp; Because of these findings, marketers now know&nbsp; that baby faces are popular with customers,&nbsp;&nbsp; but they also make sure that the baby is&nbsp; looking at what they want the customer to buy.&nbsp;&nbsp; Here is more information about the study. 2.&nbsp; Having good packaging We all know what it's&nbsp;&nbsp; like to be pulled to something because of how it&nbsp; looks. Advertisers have always known that what's&nbsp;&nbsp; inside doesn't always matter, but neuroimaging has&nbsp; taken this to a whole new level. Neuroimaging has&nbsp;&nbsp; been used to redesign the packaging of brands like&nbsp; Campbell's and Frito-Lay. In tests, customers were&nbsp;&nbsp; shown packaging and asked how they felt about it.&nbsp; Their answers were either good, bad, or neutral.&nbsp;&nbsp; Also, they were asked a lot of questions&nbsp; about the use of color, text, and images.&nbsp;&nbsp; This study showed that customers didn't like shiny&nbsp; packaging but didn't mind matte packing. Then,&nbsp;&nbsp; Frito-Lay got rid of the shiny package and&nbsp; switched to the new matte look. 107 3. Color&nbsp;&nbsp; Matters Think about how the colors you choose&nbsp; might affect how potential customers feel.&nbsp;&nbsp; Colors can make us feel a wide range of feelings,&nbsp; and studies show that some colors are linked to&nbsp;&nbsp; certain emotions. When used right, color can be&nbsp; a powerful business tool. Coca Cola's use of the&nbsp;&nbsp; color red is one of the most well-known examples,&nbsp; but there are many other companies that have also&nbsp;&nbsp; used color to great effect. Neuromarketing experts&nbsp; who study how colors work in advertising have put&nbsp;&nbsp; colors into subgroups to help people figure&nbsp; out how to use them effectively. For example,&nbsp;&nbsp; if you want to draw professionals, cool blues&nbsp; are a good choice. 4. How well ads work For a&nbsp;&nbsp; long time, studying the brain was something that&nbsp; only academics and scientists did. Neuromarketing,&nbsp;&nbsp; on the other hand, has used the amazing power of&nbsp; fMRI images to learn more about how people act&nbsp;&nbsp; and what they buy. One way that fMRI is used in&nbsp; neuromarketing is to compare advertising efforts&nbsp;&nbsp; before they are shown to the public. In one study,&nbsp; the people who took part saw three different ads&nbsp;&nbsp; for the National Cancer Institute's telephone&nbsp; number. The ad campaign that made people think&nbsp;&nbsp; the most in a certain area was the one that got&nbsp; a lot more calls to the hotline. This new way&nbsp;&nbsp; of doing things is a new way to find advertising&nbsp; efforts that will really get people interested.&nbsp;&nbsp; 5. Can't decide what to do 108 Research on how&nbsp; people act sometimes goes against what we may&nbsp;&nbsp; have thought before. Columbia University did a&nbsp; study that showed that too many options might&nbsp;&nbsp; make people not want to buy. Using different kinds&nbsp; of displays, they found that customers were less&nbsp;&nbsp; likely to stop at booths with a lot of choices.&nbsp; 6. Figuring out how happy you are EEG imaging is&nbsp;&nbsp; used in Emotion Response Analysis (ERA) to figure&nbsp; out how a person feels about a product, marketing,&nbsp;&nbsp; etc. How interested or passionate we are about&nbsp; a product is very important to the advertiser.&nbsp;&nbsp; If, for example, the customer gets very frustrated&nbsp; with your product, it's clear that there's a&nbsp;&nbsp; problem with how it works that you may want&nbsp; to fix. EEG can be used to measure how happy a&nbsp;&nbsp; customer is. In one study, EEG was used to measure&nbsp; how happy people were with a treatment for skin&nbsp;&nbsp; problems. They found that customer happiness was&nbsp; linked to activity in the parts of the brain that&nbsp;&nbsp; are used to judge facial beauty. 7. The fear of&nbsp; losing Neuromarketing has found that people really&nbsp;&nbsp; don't want to lose out, which is an interesting&nbsp; fact. People worry about what they could lose as&nbsp;&nbsp; well as what they could win. Because of this,&nbsp; "buy before it's gone" tactics work very well.&nbsp;&nbsp; When the other choice is presented as a&nbsp; loss, people are much more likely to buy.&nbsp;&nbsp; Because of this, "framing" is a very important&nbsp; idea in 109 neuromarketing. With this method,&nbsp;&nbsp; ads help people make decisions in a way that makes&nbsp; them more likely to spend money. 8. Settling down&nbsp;&nbsp; The first thing your customer learns about you is&nbsp; very important. It can help them make decisions&nbsp;&nbsp; in the future and set the tone for how they&nbsp; buy things. Neuroscientists have found a flaw&nbsp;&nbsp; in how the mind works and how it decides what&nbsp; to do. As individuals, we rarely know how much&nbsp;&nbsp; something is worth based on what it is in and of&nbsp; itself. Instead, we compare it to other choices.&nbsp;&nbsp; Using the "anchoring effect" is a good way to&nbsp; use neuromarketing because it helps people make&nbsp;&nbsp; better decisions. If two hotel rooms are&nbsp; about the same price but one comes with&nbsp;&nbsp; free coffee in the morning, you are much more&nbsp; likely to choose the one with the free coffee.&nbsp;&nbsp; You probably won't look into the quality&nbsp; of the rooms or any of the other features.&nbsp;&nbsp; Advertisers often use this to their advantage when&nbsp; comparing different deals or sets. In this way,&nbsp;&nbsp; we may often end up accepting contracts or making&nbsp; promises for a whole year. 9. The Need to Go Fast&nbsp;&nbsp; Neuromarketing is a good way to figure out what&nbsp; customers want. Companies often try to give the&nbsp;&nbsp; impression of safety and security, but customers&nbsp; may be more interested in speed and efficiency.&nbsp;&nbsp; PayPal found this out when they did a study and&nbsp; found that the promise of ease got people more&nbsp;&nbsp; excited than the promise of security. They used&nbsp; this 110 information to get more people to use&nbsp;&nbsp; their online payment service by putting the&nbsp; spotlight on how fast it was. 10. Revealing&nbsp;&nbsp; Hidden Responses In this ad, a woman played a&nbsp; joke on her friend by putting orange Cheetos in&nbsp;&nbsp; her white load of laundry. Focus groups said they&nbsp; didn't like the ad, but when the same people took&nbsp;&nbsp; part in an EEG study, it showed that they really&nbsp; liked it. People in the focus group were afraid&nbsp;&nbsp; to say that they found the ad funny out of fear&nbsp; that other people would think they were mean.&nbsp;&nbsp; In this way, neuromarketing can show thoughts&nbsp; and preferences that have been kept secret.&nbsp;&nbsp; 11. Punishment and Reward Even video game&nbsp; design has started to use psychological&nbsp;&nbsp; principles. For example, using rewards and&nbsp; punishments to make games interesting and&nbsp;&nbsp; keep people playing them is one way to use these&nbsp; principles. By making the game more rewarding,&nbsp;&nbsp; the action may also raise the amount&nbsp; of the chemical dopamine in the brain.&nbsp;&nbsp; This neurotransmitter is linked to happiness&nbsp; and good memories, which can make a person&nbsp;&nbsp; more interested in playing. Now, game designers&nbsp; even hire psychologists to help them make games,&nbsp;&nbsp; and psychological concepts are built right into&nbsp; the way the games work. 12. Testing a model&nbsp;&nbsp; Even though ads are a big part of how people&nbsp; act, the design of the goods themselves can also&nbsp;&nbsp; be important. 111 Hyundai used EEG to test their&nbsp; prototypes in a well-known case of neuromarketing.&nbsp;&nbsp; They looked at how the brain responded to&nbsp; different design features and tried to figure out&nbsp;&nbsp; what kind of stimulation made people most likely&nbsp; to buy. Based on what this study found, Hyundai&nbsp;&nbsp; changed how the cars looked from the outside. 13.&nbsp; How to Set the Price How to price things in a way&nbsp;&nbsp; that makes people want to buy them is a question&nbsp; that has been asked and debated for a long time.&nbsp;&nbsp; We all know that putting a price of $9.99 instead&nbsp; of $10 on something is a way to get people to&nbsp;&nbsp; buy it, but does it work? Several new discoveries&nbsp; are giving us more information about this age-old&nbsp;&nbsp; question. Neuromarketers are using a fascinating&nbsp; new piece of information that shows that rounded&nbsp;&nbsp; numbers are more likely to work when people&nbsp; are making decisions based on their emotions,&nbsp;&nbsp; while more complicated numbers work better&nbsp; when the logical brain is involved. This&nbsp;&nbsp; is because complex numbers make the brain&nbsp; work harder, which may make it think that&nbsp;&nbsp; the product with the more complicated price&nbsp; is the better choice. 14. Layout of a website&nbsp;&nbsp; Neuromarketing methods are also used to help plan&nbsp; the layout of websites. Neuromarketers are looking&nbsp;&nbsp; at our choices for everything from color schemes&nbsp; to layouts to font sizes and more on websites.&nbsp;&nbsp; There are now some hard and fast rules&nbsp; about how to make websites. For example,&nbsp;&nbsp; if you 112 use certificates, customer reviews,&nbsp; and social widgets, you're more likely to get&nbsp;&nbsp; customers than if you don't. Another interesting&nbsp; finding is that websites that are laid out&nbsp;&nbsp; horizontally instead of vertically work less&nbsp; well. This is because reading from the top&nbsp;&nbsp; down uses the brain and makes people more likely&nbsp; to keep scrolling. 15. Headlines That Stand Out&nbsp;&nbsp; Headlines are one of the first things people see,&nbsp; so it makes sense that they need to stand out.&nbsp;&nbsp; Because of this, they have been studied a&nbsp; lot, and a new neuromarketing method called&nbsp;&nbsp; "Hippocampal Headlines" has been created. What's&nbsp; the meaning? Researchers at University College&nbsp;&nbsp; London found that our hippocampus is activated&nbsp; when a known phrase is changed in a small way.&nbsp;&nbsp; This makes us pay attention. Many writers&nbsp; have used Patron and their slogan "Practice&nbsp;&nbsp; makes Patron" as an example of this. We&nbsp; hope these cases have been fun for you.

Yet consumers go out of their way to select these specific brands over others. - An economist would say, "How is this possible, that a rational consumer would be willing to pay more for exactly the same thing?" We love to think about ourselves as rational. That's not how it works. A very famous study done by colleagues at Duke University flashed either the Apple logo or the IBM logo to two randomized groups of participants. - The study found that after being subliminally exposed to the Apple logo, compared to when you'd been exposed to the IBM logo, participants performed better on creative tasks. - And the argument is that Apple has been telling you this story over and over again, that Apple is the brand for hip, cool, fun, creative people. - This is the true power of brands. They can influence our behavior in ways that extend way beyond the point of sale. So to what degree can the influence of brands wreak havoc on our ability to make rational spending decisions? This is your brain on money. This is Americus Reed. He studies identity and marketing at the University of Pennsylvania. When I make choices about different brands, I'm choosing to create an identity. When I put that shirt on, when I put those shoes on, those jeans, that hat, someone is going to form an impression about what I'm about. So if I'm choosing Nike over Under Armour, I'm choosing a kind of different way to express affiliation with sport. The Nike thing is about performance. The Under Armour thing is about the underdog. I have to choose which of these different conceptual pathways is most consistent with where I am in my life. - And once a consumer makes that choice, their relationship with a brand can deepen to the point where they identify with that brand like family. And once you identify with a brand, it can shape the way you behave. - And it's really interesting because they will also, if someone talks bad about that product, brand, or service, they will be the first to go out and defend. Why? Because an attack on the brand is an attack on themselves. - Michael Platt is a professor of neuroscience, marketing, and psychology whose research demonstrates how our perception of brands influences our decisions. - There's an idea in marketing, which is that we relate to brands in the same way we relate to people. It's like, "I love this brand," or, "I hate this brand." Of course, what people say, right, can often be different from what's really going on in their heads. So we thought, "Well, why don't we just ask the brain directly?" - Michael and his team observed the brains of iPhone users and Samsung Galaxy users with an MRI machine while they heard good, bad, and neutral news about Apple and Samsung. - Apple customers showed a brain empathy response toward Apple that was exactly what you'd see in the way you would respond to somebody in your own family. - Strangely, Samsung users didn't have any positive or negative responses when good or bad news was released about their brand. The only evidence that Samsung users showed was reverse empathy for Apple news. Meaning if the Apple headline was negative, their brain reflected a positive response. - You know, it really shows us that Apple has completely defined the market here. Samsung customers, it seems, from their brain data, are only buying Samsung 'cause they hate Apple. - The kicker? The Samsung users didn't report feeling the results their MRIs showed. What was happening in their brains and what they reported feeling towards Apple and Samsung, were totally different. - Most people just don't realize that they are subconsciously choosing brands because those brands have some kind of self-expressive value. - You can see there's a lot of power here in terms of shaping consumers' decisions. As we learn more and more about that, we have to think much more deeply about the ethical, legal, and societal implications of doing that. - So, as consumers, what can we do to make informed choices? Well, the best thing we can do is to be aware of the influence that brands hold. - I think it's important to always pause and think a little bit about, "Okay, why am I buying this product?" - And like it or not, brands aren't going anywhere. - I've heard lots of people push back and say that, "I'm not into brands." I take a very different view. They're not doing anything any different than what someone who affiliates with a brand is doing. They have a brand, it's just an anti-brand brand. And I think about, what is it that I've learned about identity over time? I think a lot of it has to do with the fundamental need that we as humans have to have support systems. Perhaps it was the church, it was the community, it was these other institutions that existed. Now, brands have stepped in as pillars of our identity. So I'm very much motivated to see that in that positive light.
