The consumer society is different from previous&nbsp; forms of consumption. We have a wider variety&nbsp;&nbsp; of goods and shops, more pervasive marketing,&nbsp; everything is commercialised and exchanged, and&nbsp;&nbsp; consumerism has become not just about producing&nbsp; new goods, but has become a cultural phenomenon. In his classic 1993 book Land of Desire,&nbsp;&nbsp; historian William Leach says that "The&nbsp; cardinal features of this culture were&nbsp;&nbsp; acquisition and consumption as the means of&nbsp; achieving happiness; the cult of the new;&nbsp;&nbsp; the democratisation of desire; and money value as&nbsp; the predominant measure of all value in society.’ And historian Peter Sterns defines consumerism&nbsp;&nbsp; as: ‘a society in which many people formulate&nbsp; their goals in life partly through acquiring&nbsp;&nbsp; goods that they clearly do not need for&nbsp; subsistence or for traditional display.’ So today, I want to explore our consumer world,&nbsp; our landscape of desire. What does consumerism&nbsp;&nbsp; mean? Is the term even useful? Is the West&nbsp; ‘shallow’? What does it do to us to be surrounded&nbsp;&nbsp; by image, advertising, and celebrity? Is&nbsp; consumerism making us ill, alienating us from our&nbsp;&nbsp; true selves? Is there any possibility of ethical&nbsp; or conscious consumption? Is there a way out? First, we need to look at the history of how&nbsp; consumerism developed, what we might have&nbsp;&nbsp; lost and when and why this change happened, to&nbsp; really understand what our consumer society is. Modern consumerism, as we understand it&nbsp; today, began to develop in the city states&nbsp;&nbsp; of renaissance Italy in the 15th century. Trade&nbsp; between the Far East, Middle East, and Europe&nbsp;&nbsp; increased, merchants became wealthier,&nbsp; and disposable income became more common. Artisans and shopkeepers traded&nbsp; in, owned, and collected increasing&nbsp;&nbsp; numbers of household wares like jars,&nbsp; bowls, plates, cutlery and textiles like&nbsp;&nbsp; clothes or curtains. Carvings and tapestries and&nbsp; art became more elaborate and more widespread. But the new economics of consumption&nbsp; – the newfound wealth of merchants&nbsp;&nbsp; exploring the globe - developed&nbsp; alongside an already existing moral&nbsp;&nbsp; economy in Italy that questioned consumerisms&nbsp; benefits and sought to moderate its excesses. Aristotle – whose works became more widely read&nbsp;&nbsp; during the renaissance – had argued that the&nbsp; displaying of wealth should be done virtuously.&nbsp;&nbsp; A wealthy man, he said, to be admired, should&nbsp; contribute to public works and communal feasts.&nbsp;&nbsp; Brash undirected luxury was&nbsp; immoral. It had no social use. For Plato, too, luxury led to laziness,&nbsp;&nbsp; corruption, and an inward drive for&nbsp; every increasing selfish desires. The ancient Stoics also rejected the idea of&nbsp; becoming attached to anything material and&nbsp;&nbsp; fleeting. Identifying with and becoming attached&nbsp; to an external world outside of your control would&nbsp;&nbsp; only lead to frustration when those attachments&nbsp; were challenged, perished, or were taken away.&nbsp;&nbsp; The Ancient Greeks, for the most&nbsp; part, had emphasized the inner life. The Christian Church, which of course had&nbsp; a strong presence in Renaissance Italy,&nbsp;&nbsp; adopted the values of these&nbsp; Ancient Greek philosophies. And so many in places like Florence,&nbsp; Venice and Milan were sceptical of&nbsp;&nbsp; this new commercial culture. The newly&nbsp; wealthy merchants had to ensure that&nbsp;&nbsp; their possessions were consistent with the&nbsp; conservative sensibilities of the time. In 1497, one friar started a ‘bonfire of&nbsp; vanities’ in the middle of Florence – board games,&nbsp;&nbsp; instruments, cosmetics, clothes and tapestries&nbsp; – anything that could tempt one to sin&nbsp;&nbsp; -were all burned as citizens&nbsp; danced around the bonfire. Venetians passed laws trying to regulate&nbsp; luxury, taxing spending at weddings and&nbsp;&nbsp; prohibiting certain dress styles, and&nbsp; tapestries more that 1.5m in length. As commerce thrived across Europe,&nbsp; other European states followed. In England, for example, wearing purple&nbsp; silk and gold was restricted to royals.&nbsp;&nbsp; In London in 1574, a tailor&nbsp; was sent to prison for wearing&nbsp;&nbsp; a ‘pair of hose lined with taffety, and a shirt&nbsp; edged wieth silver contrary to the ordinances’ While In much of Asia, the Buddhist tradition,&nbsp;&nbsp; much like the stoics, rejected the&nbsp; idea of attachment with possessions. It was only in the 18th century that&nbsp; these attitudes began to change. As global trade increased, people began collecting&nbsp; new and unique candlesticks, exotic linens and&nbsp;&nbsp; textiles, spices, tankards, birdcages,&nbsp; porcelains, stockings, pipes, and soaps. A taste for new foods and drinks – made&nbsp; cheaper and more abundant by the Atlantic slave&nbsp;&nbsp; trade – increased and consumers became addicted&nbsp; to coffee, tea, chocolate, and especially sugar. Cotton from plants – again, made cheaper with&nbsp; slave labour - instead of animals were cheaper,&nbsp;&nbsp; took dyes better and suddenly clothes&nbsp; became more colourful and more varied. All of this coincided with the&nbsp; development of modern marketing,&nbsp;&nbsp; advertising, and salesmanship as merchants&nbsp; sought new ways to promote new goods. English pottery maker Josiah Wedgwood invented&nbsp; the modern salesman in the 18th century. As historian Neil McKendrick writes Wedgwood used: ‘inertia-selling campaigns, product&nbsp; differentiation, market segmentation,&nbsp;&nbsp; detailed market research, embryonic self-service&nbsp; schemes, money-back-if-not-satisfied policies,&nbsp;&nbsp; free carriage, giveaway sales promotions,&nbsp; auctions, lotteries, catalogues… advanced credit,&nbsp;&nbsp; three-tier discount schemes, including major&nbsp; discounts for first orders, and almost every&nbsp;&nbsp; form of advertisement, trade cards, shop signs,&nbsp; letterheads, bill heads, newspaper and magazine&nbsp;&nbsp; advertisements, fashion plates and fashion&nbsp; magazines, solicited puffs, organized propaganda&nbsp;&nbsp; campaigns, even false attacks organized to produce&nbsp; the opportunity to publicize the counterattack ‘ Throughout the 19th century consumerism&nbsp; continued entering the home.&nbsp;&nbsp; In Britain, a new trend - Wallpaper led&nbsp; to sales going through the roof. Art,&nbsp;&nbsp; photography, and miniature replicas&nbsp; of statues and ornaments became&nbsp;&nbsp; cheaper to reproduce and manufacture.&nbsp; Clocks and watches became more popular. Then, glass windows were invented. Shop windows, glass cabinets and displays created&nbsp; a new relationship between the consumer good&nbsp;&nbsp; and the consumer. ‘Perhaps more than any other&nbsp; medium,’the historian JW Lungstrum writes, ‘glass&nbsp;&nbsp; democratized desire even as it&nbsp; democratized access to goods.’ And in the 20th century,&nbsp; DIY, tools, commercial music,&nbsp;&nbsp; radio, cinema, and television, technology&nbsp; and gadgets and computers supercharged the&nbsp;&nbsp; consumer revolution. McDonald opened its doors&nbsp; in 1955. Credit cards were introduced in 1958.&nbsp;&nbsp; Comic books and Hollywood, Microsoft,&nbsp; and Apple, took over the world. Supermarkets and shopping malls sprang up and&nbsp; governments invested in highways to connect them.&nbsp;&nbsp; In 1946 there were just 8 suburban&nbsp; shopping centres in the US,&nbsp;&nbsp; 14 years later in 1960 there were almost 4000. These new cathedrals of commerce&nbsp; epitomised the shift in culture.&nbsp;&nbsp; Famed architect Victor Gruen designed the largest&nbsp; shopping mall in the world in Detroit in 1952.&nbsp;&nbsp; It had a hundred stores, private roads, a&nbsp; power plant, a police force, a water system,&nbsp;&nbsp; and was designed as a self-contained city. Gruen’s&nbsp; next project in Minnesota was even more ambitious.&nbsp;&nbsp; He designed it so that deliveries, the organising&nbsp; of stock, the wires & pipes were accessed from the&nbsp;&nbsp; back, hidden from view, so that everything&nbsp; appeared on the shelves as if by magic. Gruen believed that these new developments could&nbsp; be the hearts of the new suburban communities&nbsp;&nbsp; that were springing up, that were in desperate&nbsp; need of a kind of spiritual communal core. Later&nbsp;&nbsp; in life he became appalled at how they turned&nbsp; out. He wrote that instead of providing the “need,&nbsp;&nbsp; place and opportunity for participation in&nbsp; modern community life that the ancient Greek&nbsp;&nbsp; Agora, the Medieval Market and Place, and&nbsp; our own Town Squares provided in the past,”&nbsp;&nbsp; they’d become ‘bastard developments’. He&nbsp; retired to Vienna, becoming a science fiction&nbsp;&nbsp; commenting on the environmental destruction&nbsp; our new suburban culture was causing. So while consumerism developed over centuries,&nbsp; the postwar consumer revolution – the one we’re&nbsp;&nbsp; all a product of and living in right now&nbsp; - was a fundamental break from the past.&nbsp;&nbsp; Mass consumption became national, international,&nbsp;&nbsp; advertising pervaded every living room through&nbsp; radio and television and then the internet.&nbsp;&nbsp; Disposable income increased (for many). Rock and&nbsp; roll, birth control, and the swinging sixties made&nbsp;&nbsp; hedonism and the enjoyment of new desires,&nbsp; respectable. But if consumerism is so broad,&nbsp;&nbsp; so vague, so far-reaching, what,&nbsp; really, does a consumer society mean? Ok, so we’ve looked at some history,&nbsp;&nbsp; what about the culture, the psychology, the&nbsp; sociology, the philosophy or consumerism. There is clearly not one single consumerism,&nbsp; though. We consume everything from food to music,&nbsp;&nbsp; to essential oils to new package experiences.&nbsp; Is it all just hedonistic? No, clearly not, we&nbsp;&nbsp; consume books and audio books and online lectures,&nbsp; we consume healthy foods we don’t necessarily&nbsp;&nbsp; enjoy, we use gadgets like sports watches&nbsp; that we don’t necessarily get pleasure from. But consumerism is even more complicated.&nbsp; It’s not just stuff. It’s a cultural activity,&nbsp;&nbsp; a subject, certain attitude towards the&nbsp; world. We have to remember that ‘going&nbsp;&nbsp; shopping’ and ‘being a consumer’ is a&nbsp; historical cultural activity that has&nbsp;&nbsp; norms – that’s done in different ways depending&nbsp; on the person, the place, the historical period.&nbsp;&nbsp; Its not just the act of purchasing and&nbsp; consumption – its the perspectives,&nbsp;&nbsp; the specific activities, the marketing,&nbsp; the relationships that go with it. Consumer groups and cooperatives&nbsp; and political parties and pressure&nbsp;&nbsp; groups and lobbies all developed&nbsp; throughout the 19the century.&nbsp;&nbsp; Consumers organized, there are book genres&nbsp; and discourses about shopping conscientiously,&nbsp;&nbsp; consumer groups lobby the states&nbsp; for rights and consumer protections. So apart from the obvious – an increase in&nbsp; global trade, the black death played a huge role,&nbsp;&nbsp; by the way – so many died that the people&nbsp; that survived were better off financially&nbsp;&nbsp; and had more disposable income – apart from this&nbsp; stuff, can we identify any cultural dynamics that&nbsp;&nbsp; might help us understand consumerism today?&nbsp; I think there are two that provide a good&nbsp;&nbsp; route into the psychology and sociology: the&nbsp; production of new desires and social mimicry. Some objects – some consumer goods,&nbsp; fulfill a simple natural biological&nbsp;&nbsp; need – we eat to satiate ourselves,&nbsp; we buy a bed to sleep on, a home&nbsp;&nbsp; to protect us from the elements. But&nbsp; we’re not just a needs species, we go&nbsp;&nbsp; beyond our simple needs, create new&nbsp; desires, new ways of being in the world. We seem to have a desire for the new&nbsp; – but really understanding what that&nbsp;&nbsp; means, has only developed over&nbsp; the past few hundred years. We can see this shift in what desire&nbsp; means across the 19th century. Sociologist Colin Campbell argues, for example&nbsp; that, Romanticism – that hugely influential&nbsp;&nbsp; pan-European movement that emphasised feelings,&nbsp; sentiments, emotions, novel experiences and&nbsp;&nbsp; adventure and creativity – was an important part&nbsp; of the development of the consumerism outlook. He wrote that the consumer ‘‘withdraw(s)&nbsp; from reality as fast as he encounters it,&nbsp;&nbsp; ever-casting his day-dreams forward in time,&nbsp; attaching them to objects of desire, and then&nbsp;&nbsp; subsequently “unhooking” them from these objects&nbsp; as and when they are attained and experienced’. As modernity developed and we were unshackled from&nbsp; the circularity of traditional life, of the same&nbsp;&nbsp; routines every day, month, and year, we began&nbsp; to want to collect something new: experiences. Oscar Wilde satirised this idea of new&nbsp; experiences in hi 1891 The Picture of Dorian Gray.&nbsp;&nbsp; Dorian exchanges his soul for everlasting youth&nbsp; so that he can live endlessly as a hedonist. As Rachel Bowlby writes that Gray ‘exchanges&nbsp; his moral self for the unbounded liberty&nbsp;&nbsp; of the new hedonist’, there is no limit to&nbsp; ‘to the number of personalities he can adopt,&nbsp;&nbsp; to the experiences he can try.’ The modern world created adventurers, explorers,&nbsp;&nbsp; dandies, and flaneurs, moving through the&nbsp; world just to collate and understand the new. Already in 1655, philosopher and scientist&nbsp; Robert Boyle had written that while&nbsp;&nbsp; ‘other creatures were content with&nbsp; easily attainable necessaries’,&nbsp;&nbsp; humans had ‘a multiplicity of&nbsp; desires’ and ‘greedy appetites.’ In 1741’s Fable of the Bees, Bernard Mandeville&nbsp; had argued against the received wisdom of&nbsp;&nbsp; Christianity, the Ancient Greeks and the Romans&nbsp; that private vice and selfish individual desire&nbsp;&nbsp; were pernicious. Instead, he said, they were&nbsp; socially useful - they created more trade,&nbsp;&nbsp; more commerce, and in the&nbsp; end made everyone better off. Scottish Enlightenment philosopher&nbsp; David Hume agreed to an extent&nbsp;&nbsp; writing that indolent luxury was still pernicious&nbsp; but that an ‘increase and consumption of all the&nbsp;&nbsp; commodities, which serve to the ornament and&nbsp; pleasures of life, are advantages to society’. When Wilde was writing in the 19th century,&nbsp; Paris was becoming an international a hotspot&nbsp;&nbsp; for new department stores placing a&nbsp; universe of exotic goods on display In The Ladies Paradise, Emile Zola wrote about&nbsp; the allure of the new stores. He called them&nbsp;&nbsp; ‘alters’ – a miracle – a ‘machine’ – and that&nbsp; ‘mad desires were driving all the women crazy. ‘ Other Parisians and critics talked about the new&nbsp; type of person: the flaneur – the person strolling&nbsp;&nbsp; aimlessly around the Parisian arcades, taking&nbsp; it all in, experiencing as much as possible. At the beginning of the 20th century, as&nbsp; Henry Ford popularized a new method of&nbsp;&nbsp; standarsized mass production, capitalists&nbsp; and then advertising executives on Madison&nbsp;&nbsp; Avenue wondered how new desires could be&nbsp; maintained, even created from thin air. The father of public relations and&nbsp; Freud’s nephew, Edward Bernays wrote that "Mass production is profitable only if its&nbsp;&nbsp; rhythm can be maintained." Business&nbsp; "cannot afford to wait until the public&nbsp;&nbsp; asks for its product; it must maintain constant&nbsp; touch, through advertising and propaganda…&nbsp;&nbsp; to assure itself the continuous demand which&nbsp; alone will make its costly plant profitable". Freud became central to the new advertising&nbsp; industry. Ad men drew on his theories of&nbsp;&nbsp; sexual desire, oral gratification, and&nbsp; the pleasure principle to sell new brands. The psychologist and marketer&nbsp; Ernest Dichter famously recommended:&nbsp;&nbsp; ‘don’t sell shoes – sell lovely feet!’ The shift was that consumerism&nbsp; and the marketing that was&nbsp;&nbsp; developing with it wasn't about needs&nbsp; it was about new fantasies, new lives,&nbsp;&nbsp; becoming a new and different person. It wasnt&nbsp; about the present, it was about the future. Lehman Brother’s Paul Mazur wrote that: "We must shift America from a&nbsp; needs, to a desires culture.&nbsp;&nbsp; People must be trained to desire, to want new&nbsp; things even before the old had been entirely&nbsp;&nbsp; consumed. We must shape a new mentality in&nbsp; America. Man's desires must overshadow his needs." Some of these new desires, new dreams and&nbsp; visions were practical – the washing machine&nbsp;&nbsp; freeing up the housewife’s time,&nbsp; the automobile, the typewriter–&nbsp;&nbsp; others were criticised as luxuries –&nbsp; sports cars and endless new fashions. Retail analyst Victor Lebow wrote in 1955:&nbsp; "Our enormously productive economy demands&nbsp;&nbsp; that we make consumption our way of life, that we&nbsp; convert the buying and use of goods into rituals,&nbsp;&nbsp; that we seek our spiritual satisfaction, our&nbsp; ego satisfaction, in consumption.… We need&nbsp;&nbsp; things consumed, burned up, replaced and&nbsp; discarded at an ever-accelerating rate." The landscape of desire was&nbsp; were production and consumption,&nbsp;&nbsp; marketing, advertising and the individual met. As the philosopher Jean Baurillard –&nbsp; who will come to shortly - points out&nbsp;&nbsp; in his classic The Consumer Society, heroes&nbsp; of production – colonizers, explorers,&nbsp;&nbsp; founders, industrialists – gave way to heroes&nbsp; of consumption – celebrities, gilded princes,&nbsp;&nbsp; and sports stars – notable figures that wore&nbsp; the latest designs and drove the flashiest cars. But we don’t just consume&nbsp; alone. We don’t invent our&nbsp;&nbsp; own desires independently. Those figures&nbsp; – the heroes of consumption – and our&nbsp;&nbsp; social life more broadly provide models for&nbsp; mimicry. We’re an inherently social species. In the old Royal Courts of Europe, adopting&nbsp; conspicuous styles stood one out from your&nbsp;&nbsp; competitors. Now, celebrities and models set&nbsp; trends, but we all like to be ahead of the pack. In 1899, the sociologist Thorstein&nbsp; Veblen coined the term ‘conspicuous&nbsp;&nbsp; consumption’ to describe the upper class&nbsp; phenomenon of buying, displaying, and&nbsp;&nbsp; wearing luxury goods to distinguish&nbsp; themselves from their peers. In 1950, the economist Harvey Leibenstein adapted&nbsp; the idea of conspicuous consumption – he noted&nbsp;&nbsp; how not only did the wealthy adopt new styles to&nbsp; set themselves apart, but that the middle classes&nbsp;&nbsp; then copied them to try and display social&nbsp; status. He called it the bandwagon effect. The Veblen effect – as its come to be known –&nbsp; means that the aquiring of consumer goods is&nbsp;&nbsp; not just about use, utility, beauty, boredom,&nbsp; or innovation – but about status. The value of&nbsp;&nbsp; the good is not determined by its usefulness&nbsp; but by the social value of displaying it. But status is not just a surface phenomenon– being&nbsp; in the know is about having the right knowledge,&nbsp;&nbsp; the right know-how, knowing the direction of the&nbsp; wind. It’s all necessary to being accepted in the&nbsp;&nbsp; correct circles, whether that’s about class,&nbsp; or being a fashion designer or an inventor.&nbsp;&nbsp; Even science has fashionable trends. As the sociologist Roberta&nbsp; Sassatelli writes there is ‘‘the knowledge (gastronomic or social)&nbsp; that derives from having eaten out,&nbsp;&nbsp; tasted this or that dish, having used a given&nbsp; type of cutlery, and having managed well the&nbsp;&nbsp; phases of the meal, that is tasting, commenting on&nbsp; the dishes, chatting and exchanging information.” This act of social mimicry&nbsp; functions in a strange way,&nbsp;&nbsp; almost as if its an engine. Often, once the vulgar&nbsp; lesser lower classes begin to adopt a style,&nbsp;&nbsp; then it no longer distinguishes the upper&nbsp; classes who brought it into fashion and used&nbsp;&nbsp; it to distinguish themselves as unique,&nbsp; as special. And so trends keep revolving&nbsp;&nbsp; as a new new trend setters turn away&nbsp; from the crowd and adopt new styles. The sociologist Georg Simmel writes that: ‘As soon&nbsp; as the lower classes begin to copy their style,&nbsp;&nbsp; thereby crossing the line of the demarcation&nbsp; the upper classes have drawn and destroying the&nbsp;&nbsp; uniformity of their coherence, the upper classes&nbsp; turn away from this style and adopt a new one,&nbsp;&nbsp; which in turn differentiated them from the&nbsp; masses; and thus the game goes merrily on.’ Baudrillard argued that in the postwar consumer&nbsp; society not only is their conspicuous consumption&nbsp;&nbsp; but a ‘fantastic conspicuousness.’ We’re&nbsp; everywhere surrounded by styles and images&nbsp;&nbsp; to imitate, new gadgets to employ, and the&nbsp; turnover rate for new fashions is inexorable. Ok, so consumerism is about creating new desires&nbsp; and social mimicry. But, you might be wondering,&nbsp;&nbsp; what's bad about this? Where’s the problem? I&nbsp; buy new camera equipment, lights, microphones,&nbsp;&nbsp; books – I have a bike that would be impossible&nbsp; to manufacture only twenty years ago.&nbsp;&nbsp; All of them are desires that have been&nbsp; created and, well, I watch reviews and&nbsp;&nbsp; see what photographers use etc, so its social&nbsp; mimicry. But I find all this stuff useful.&nbsp;&nbsp; I find the task I use them for meaningful, and&nbsp; I hope you do to. So again, where’s the problem? We can categorise the problems critics&nbsp; have identified into two parts: One is quite simple. Consumption per se isnt bad,&nbsp; but its side-effects, its unintended consequences,&nbsp;&nbsp; certain types of consumption, are. They are&nbsp; things like addiction, environmental degradation,&nbsp;&nbsp; exploitative labour practices, off-shoring, etc. I’ll return to these issues shortly. The&nbsp; other problem critics have identified is&nbsp;&nbsp; more philosophical, sociological, and&nbsp; psychological – it’s that consumerism&nbsp;&nbsp; effects us in our very psyches – we have a&nbsp; modern consumer mentality, and its out of joint. One touchstone for this type of critique&nbsp; is the economist Kenneth Galbraith’s The&nbsp;&nbsp; Affluent Society published in 1958.&nbsp; Galbraith argued that now that very&nbsp;&nbsp; basic needs of most Americans had been met,&nbsp; new demands had to be created artificially. Growth required consumption and so&nbsp; it was the job of capitalists to be&nbsp;&nbsp; endlessly creating new desires to keep people&nbsp; running circuitously around the hamster wheel. He argued that our postwar society was one&nbsp; addicted to consumption at the expense of&nbsp;&nbsp; social and political problem. In a consumer&nbsp; society, dominated by industry, growth is the&nbsp;&nbsp; central goal. There is, he says, an ‘inherently&nbsp; unstable process of consumer debt creation’,&nbsp;&nbsp; as people borrowed more and more on credit cards.&nbsp; The focus on private goods produced ‘private&nbsp;&nbsp; opulence and public squalor’ as people became&nbsp; more hedonistic and neglected their communities,&nbsp;&nbsp; civic society, and environments. He described&nbsp; people driving their ‘mauve and cerise,&nbsp;&nbsp; airconditioned, power-steered, and power-braked&nbsp; automobile’ through badly paved streets to have&nbsp;&nbsp; picnic of ‘exquisitely packaged food from&nbsp; a portable icebox by a polluted stream.’ Because we become so focused on consumption,&nbsp; other values become marginalised. We can understand this as a critique in&nbsp; the tradition of what’s often been called&nbsp;&nbsp; alienation. Karl Marx had argued that&nbsp; capitalism alienates us from our true&nbsp;&nbsp; species being. We fetishise commodities because of&nbsp; their monetary exchange value, which covers up the&nbsp;&nbsp; social processes that went into the manufacture&nbsp; of the product. We see the world through the lens&nbsp;&nbsp; of a cash nexus which covers up what’s&nbsp; really going on under the surface. Arguments about and definitions of alienation&nbsp; have taken many forms, but its most accessible&nbsp;&nbsp; popular understanding is that&nbsp; we buy stuff we don’t need,&nbsp;&nbsp; sold by adverts we don’t want to see, that&nbsp; make us desirous of things we need to desire,&nbsp;&nbsp; in an addictive society that distorts&nbsp; and discounts our true needs. In his book Empire of Things, historian Frank&nbsp; Trentmann argues that we used to see ourselves&nbsp;&nbsp; as part of the world – more holistically - and&nbsp; that the entire world and our experience of it&nbsp;&nbsp; was thought of more organically, more&nbsp; immediately, more sacredly, even. He says though that this was ‘torn asunder&nbsp; by René Descartes, who, in the 1640s,&nbsp;&nbsp; argued that the mind was an entity separate from&nbsp; the body and the material world. A century and&nbsp;&nbsp; a half later, Immanuel Kant is said to have&nbsp; completed ‘humankind’s victory over things’. What this means is that many philosophers&nbsp; of the Enlightenment argued that we could&nbsp;&nbsp; stand apart from the world, rationalise it,&nbsp; calculate it logically, see things objectively. This shift contributed to our mistaken belief&nbsp; that we could simply control the world around us,&nbsp;&nbsp; that we could manipulate and collect and examine&nbsp; objects and, as a consequence, consumer goods. Of course, we know this is a mistake. Things&nbsp; have an effect on us, the world around us has&nbsp;&nbsp; an effect on us, no matter how much we try to be&nbsp; the owner of our stuff, our stuff, in many ways,&nbsp;&nbsp; become the owners of us – they determine what we&nbsp; think, how we perceive ourselves, what we do. They&nbsp;&nbsp; can turn us into addicts, they can frustrate&nbsp; us, they can lead us down routes that aren’t&nbsp;&nbsp; good for us without us even knowing it. That’s&nbsp; the alienation argument. We’re a sick society. Marx called religion an opiate of the masses.&nbsp; It kept people docile, easily controlled,&nbsp;&nbsp; under the thumb of their rulers, distracted&nbsp; from the real problems around them. Now,&nbsp;&nbsp; many have argued, consumerism has&nbsp; become the opiate of the masses. The Enlish novelist J.B Presitly bemoaned&nbsp; in the middle of the 20th century that&nbsp;&nbsp; Britain was becoming like ‘Southern&nbsp; California, with its TV and film studios,&nbsp;&nbsp; automobile way of life (you can eat&nbsp; and drink, watch films, make love,&nbsp;&nbsp; without ever getting out of your car), its&nbsp; flavourless cosmopolitanism .and bogus religions.’ Or take this quote from Frankmann’s Empire&nbsp; of Things on a cinema goer from the 1920s: ‘One young British woman, a shorthand typist&nbsp; who went to the pictures four times a week,&nbsp;&nbsp; found that seeing ‘marvellous places’ like&nbsp; New York and California on the screen left her&nbsp;&nbsp; ‘miserable and unhappy sitting in my stuffy little&nbsp; office all day with nobody to talk to but myself&nbsp;&nbsp; (which I don’t) and to go home to a house that&nbsp; should have been knocked down five years ago.’ These quotes suggest that what we’re surrounded&nbsp; by is somehow wrong. That we’re subjected to&nbsp;&nbsp; and forced to absorb and embody great images of&nbsp; desires that we don’t have but others – mysterious&nbsp;&nbsp; others, often out of reach, often manipulated&nbsp; and polished to sell more adverts –&nbsp;&nbsp; do. The images aren’t real, they’re not&nbsp; representative of reality, they have no depth. The postmodern consumer society&nbsp; is associated with the MTV viewer,&nbsp;&nbsp; channel hopping, flipping through images with&nbsp; an easily accessible remote, listening to&nbsp;&nbsp; disjointed sounds and flashing images&nbsp; without really feeling anything. The viewer, in sociologist&nbsp; Mike Featherstone's words,&nbsp;&nbsp; ‘merely enjoys the multiphrenic intensities&nbsp; and sensations of the surface of the images.’ It’s all connected. Because flipping through MTV&nbsp; works through the same logic as fast-fashion and&nbsp;&nbsp; gadgets with built in obsolescence:&nbsp; its all fleeting, nothing lasts,&nbsp;&nbsp; quality diminishes – it’s designed so that you&nbsp; consume it quickly and move on to the next thing. This is a common critique of a postmodern&nbsp; culture that the some say underpins our consume&nbsp;&nbsp; culture. If you look at art, literature,&nbsp; and film they jump around stylistically. Fast-fashion trends come and go, styles in fashion&nbsp; and film are just stuck together in pastiche,&nbsp;&nbsp; the world moves so fast that nothing&nbsp; can be properly understood, analysed,&nbsp;&nbsp; critiqued – there is, in the philosopher Fredric&nbsp; Jameson's’ words, a depthlessness to our world. It’s driven by production and consumption but&nbsp; psychologises us by infecting our culture too. The Frankfurt School philosophers Adorno and&nbsp; Horkheimer argued that Hollywood and the wider&nbsp;&nbsp; culture industry that developed across the&nbsp; 20th century was shallow – everything was&nbsp;&nbsp; standardised to reduce costs and commodified&nbsp; to reach the widest consumer market.&nbsp;&nbsp; All culture – music, fashion, art, film –&nbsp; was reduced to the lowest common denominator&nbsp;&nbsp; so that it could be consumed by&nbsp; the largest number of consumers. They write, ‘culture today is infecting everything&nbsp; with sameness. Film, radio, and magazines forms&nbsp;&nbsp; a system. Each branch of culture is unanimous&nbsp; within itself and all are unanimous together. Each character can pop up&nbsp; interchangeably in each film.&nbsp;&nbsp; Ironman and Captain America can be&nbsp; replaced with new incarnations. Each new&nbsp;&nbsp; storyline in a television is easily recognisable.&nbsp; The same types of humour resonate throughout. And&nbsp;&nbsp; product placement is everywhere. It is simple. Easy. Consumable.&nbsp; We can see similar arguments in three more&nbsp; thinkers: Fredrich Jameson, Jean Baudrillard,&nbsp;&nbsp; and David Harvey. They all put emphasis on the&nbsp; culture of our postmodern consumer society too.&nbsp;&nbsp; That its obsessed with image, with&nbsp; shallowness and lack of depth. I want to quickly go through each one, because&nbsp; there are similarities in them that can help us&nbsp;&nbsp; understand what unifies many of the critiques&nbsp; and so we can then etter think about solutions.&nbsp;&nbsp; We’ll then turn to what they might&nbsp; have left out, what criticisms of&nbsp;&nbsp; them are, before trying to think&nbsp; about consumerism in a new way. Jean Baudrillard published the&nbsp; Consumer Society in 1970. I love&nbsp;&nbsp; this quote that really encapsulates the FOMO&nbsp; of consumerism, how forward looking he was.&nbsp;&nbsp; He wrote that consumerism came with a ‘revival&nbsp; of a universal curiosity in respect of cookery,&nbsp;&nbsp; culture, science, religion, sexuality, etc. 'Try&nbsp; Jesus!' runs an American slogan. You have to try&nbsp;&nbsp; everything, for consumerist man is haunted by&nbsp; the fear of 'missing' something, some form of&nbsp;&nbsp; enjoyment or other. You never know whether a&nbsp; particular encounter, a particular experience&nbsp;&nbsp; (Christmas in the Canaries, eel in whisky,&nbsp; the Prado, LSD, Japanese-style love-making)&nbsp;&nbsp; will not elicit some 'sensation'. It is no&nbsp; longer desire, or even 'taste', or a specific&nbsp;&nbsp; inclination that are at stake, but a generalized&nbsp; curiosity, driven by a vague sense of unease.’ Baudrillard was concerned primarily with image&nbsp; and language – the signs of consumer advertising&nbsp;&nbsp; and commercial language. He talked about&nbsp; the dizzying abundance of those signs,&nbsp;&nbsp; and argued that we were so saturated&nbsp; in the language of consumerism&nbsp;&nbsp; that that language dominated our lives more than&nbsp; any other way of communicating with each other. He wrote: ‘There is all around us today a kind&nbsp; of fantastic conspicuousness of consumption and&nbsp;&nbsp; abundance, constituted by the multiplication&nbsp; of objects, services and material goods,&nbsp;&nbsp; and this represents something of a fundamental&nbsp; mutation in the ecology of the human species.’ For Marx, under capitalism, what he called the&nbsp; ‘use value’ of an object – the real value of what&nbsp;&nbsp; its worth to me and us societally to use this mug,&nbsp; say – had been been replaced in our heads with&nbsp;&nbsp; an exchange value – we think instead about how&nbsp; much an item is worth economically. For example,&nbsp;&nbsp; someone might like this mug because it cost a lot&nbsp; of money and has diamonds implanted in the rim,&nbsp;&nbsp; not because they like it aesthetically&nbsp; or think its the perfect size.&nbsp;&nbsp; Fetishising commodities in this way also&nbsp; hides the social labour, the real work,&nbsp;&nbsp; the real lives, that went into making the&nbsp; object. We simply think of it market terms. On top of use value and exchange value,&nbsp;&nbsp; Baudrillard added a third value: sign value.&nbsp; We value things not by how useful they are,&nbsp;&nbsp; or even how much we can get for them, but&nbsp; on what they signify to others socially.&nbsp;&nbsp; I might like this mug, for example,&nbsp; because it’s a fashionable Ted Baker mug. Baudrillard argued that this sign value&nbsp; was like a hidden language we all speak. We live in a network of brand names,&nbsp; consumer images, movie stars with new shoes,&nbsp;&nbsp; and social status that depends largely&nbsp; on where we live, what we own, what our&nbsp;&nbsp; position is at work – and all of these things have&nbsp; a direct effect on what we value, what we desire,&nbsp;&nbsp; and what these things say about us to others.&nbsp; Baudrillard called this network a code,&nbsp;&nbsp; and he said we were more concerned with the&nbsp; code than we were with reality – the real He sees this consumer code as being like a&nbsp; language that speaks to us. We don’t desire&nbsp;&nbsp; new things at random – desires must be created,&nbsp; coded, they must fit into the system of fantasy.&nbsp;&nbsp; New goods must somehow be inserted&nbsp; into the existing order of consumption. Our desires aren’t just&nbsp; biological, personal, individual,&nbsp;&nbsp; or based on use-value – usefulness – or exchange&nbsp; value – that this is a gold plated laptop so&nbsp;&nbsp; will be worth more – but are&nbsp; socially constructed. We are coded&nbsp;&nbsp; to desire socially depending on others,&nbsp; and this determines how we think. Our needs aren’t rational, nor are they&nbsp; even about maximising utility. Social power&nbsp;&nbsp; rules. We are socialized, culturalised,&nbsp; consumerised by an abundance of&nbsp;&nbsp; messages, flashing lights, screens and magazines. What drives this? Baudrillard returns in many ways&nbsp; to Veblen’s theory of conspicuous consumption.&nbsp;&nbsp; We want to distinguish ourselves,&nbsp; setting ourselves apart socially. He calls this a ‘dialectic of&nbsp; conformism and originality’.&nbsp;&nbsp; We both want to conform – be part of the pack&nbsp; – and be original – stand outside the pack. There is, Baudrillard says,&nbsp; ‘a 'need of the individual to&nbsp;&nbsp; differentiate himself' as one more element&nbsp; in the repertoire of individual needs,&nbsp;&nbsp; which it sees as alternating with&nbsp; the opposite need to conform.’ Manufacturers want to fit these new desires – this&nbsp;&nbsp; code – into our lives without continuously&nbsp; upending their whole manufacturing lines. Modern furniture is designed to be flexible,&nbsp;&nbsp; mobile, interchangeable, without depth so it&nbsp; can fit in different spaces and be moved easily.&nbsp;&nbsp; Everything is in neutral colours and like&nbsp; IKEA, fits together like a puzzle, like a code. Tradition, uniqueness, odd&nbsp; shapes, personal history&nbsp;&nbsp; is no-longer important in the home. It’s about&nbsp; flatness, neutralness, every home looks the same. Apple resembles this, resembles IKEA. You’re&nbsp; sold a new Mac and now you need an iPad, iPhone,&nbsp;&nbsp; iWatch, airpods. And, if you don’t have apple,&nbsp;&nbsp; you need one because you might be left out,&nbsp; you can’t use iChat, you can’t send photos&nbsp;&nbsp; easily to your friends – the consumer code&nbsp; draws you in – if not, you’re ostracised. Baudrillard says, anticipating Apple,&nbsp;&nbsp; ‘Few objects today are offered alone,&nbsp; without a context of objects which&nbsp;&nbsp; 'speaks' them.’ - shop-windows, adverts, brand&nbsp; names, all come together in a cohesive vision.’ Baudrillard is famously pessimistic about&nbsp; this state of affairs. He argues we’re&nbsp;&nbsp; so soaked in this culture that we can no&nbsp; longer discover our true authentic needs. Everything is alienated because everything can&nbsp; be exchanged away. Nothing is transcendental.&nbsp;&nbsp; Everything is pastiche – the car advert relies&nbsp; on the sunglasses, the sunglasses are sold with&nbsp;&nbsp; holiday packages, the dream is a holiday in&nbsp; bermuda because that’s where Brad Pitt went –&nbsp;&nbsp; all of these phenomena build, construct,&nbsp; and direct your desires – but true meaning,&nbsp;&nbsp; what we really need, is lost. He uses the example of Kitsch&nbsp; products to illustrate what we means. Kitsch goods are everywhere. They’re 'trashy&nbsp; objects', 'folksy knick-knacks', 'souvenirs',&nbsp;&nbsp; he says. But they’re shallow imitations.&nbsp; They’re no longer connected to the real reason,&nbsp;&nbsp; the original reason, the piece of art or&nbsp; historical building they imitate was produced.&nbsp;&nbsp; Kitsche is the ultimate in artificial desire. HE writes: ‘Kitsch can be anywhere: in&nbsp; the detail of an object or in the plan&nbsp;&nbsp; of a new residential area, in an artificial flower&nbsp; or in a photo-novel. It can best be defined as&nbsp;&nbsp; a pseudo-object or, in other words,&nbsp; as a simulation, a copy, an imitation,&nbsp;&nbsp; a stereotype, as a dearth of real&nbsp; signification and a superabundance of signs.’ They are just ‘part of the package,&nbsp; the constellation of accessories by&nbsp;&nbsp; which the 'socio-cultural' standing&nbsp; of the average citizen is determined.’ Pop art functions in a similar way. Its all&nbsp; surface, it uses the signifiers of the world&nbsp;&nbsp; around us, and slaps it together, ignoring&nbsp; the true deep meaning that’s been hidden. He says: ‘Whereas all art up to pop was based&nbsp; on a 'depth' vision of the world, pop regards&nbsp;&nbsp; itself as homogeneous with this immanent order&nbsp; of signs: homogeneous with their industrial,&nbsp;&nbsp; mass production and hence with the artificial,&nbsp; manufactured character of the whole environment.’ WE see a similar same critique of the shallowness&nbsp; of our postmodern landscape in the American&nbsp;&nbsp; philosopher Fredric Jameson. His essay, turned&nbsp; into a book, ‘Postmodernism, or the Cultural Logic&nbsp;&nbsp; of Late Capitalism’, published in 1984, has been&nbsp; called the most discussed article of the 1980s. For Jameson, there is a particular&nbsp; reason consumer culture is shallow. He writes that our postmodern culture&nbsp; is schizophrenic, it jumps from place&nbsp;&nbsp; to place – and relies on ‘a new depthlessness,&nbsp; which finds its prolongation both in contemporary&nbsp;&nbsp; “theory” and in a whole new culture of the&nbsp; image’ and the ‘weakening of historicity,&nbsp;&nbsp; both in our relationship to public History and&nbsp; in the new forms of our private temporality.’ He argues culture has become so&nbsp; shallow that our relationship&nbsp;&nbsp; to the depth of history has been lost. Culture is fragmented because capitalism&nbsp; is fragmented. We are detached from&nbsp;&nbsp; everything because we have to be – styles&nbsp; change, trends change, conditions change,&nbsp;&nbsp; jobs change, information changes quicker&nbsp; than we can keep up, and so we’re&nbsp;&nbsp; psychologically schizophrenic,&nbsp; frantically trying to keep up. Jameson famously compares Van Gogh’s a&nbsp; pair of boots from 1887 – a modernist&nbsp;&nbsp; painting – with Andy Worholls&nbsp; postmodern 1980 Diamond Dust Shoes. He argues that Van Gogh’s shoes&nbsp; are connected to a real world. He says ‘‘the whole missing object world which&nbsp; was once [the shoes’] lived context. . .the heavy&nbsp;&nbsp; tread of the peasant woman, the loneliness&nbsp; of the field path, the hut in the clearing,&nbsp;&nbsp; the worn and broken instruments of&nbsp; labor in the furrows and at the hearth’ ON the other hand ‘Andy Warhol’s Diamond Dust&nbsp; Shoes evidently no longer speaks to us with any&nbsp;&nbsp; of the immediacy of Van Gogh’s footgear; indeed,&nbsp; I am tempted to say that it does not really speak&nbsp;&nbsp; to us at all. Nothing in this painting organizes&nbsp; even a minimal place for the viewer. . .We are&nbsp;&nbsp; witnessing the emergence of a new kind of flatness&nbsp; or depthlessness, a new kind of superficiality.’ He says the same process is visible in our broad&nbsp; cultural understanding of the Vietnam war. He says&nbsp;&nbsp; its shaped not by reality, not by real history&nbsp; or understanding, but by Hollywood films, protest&nbsp;&nbsp; music, flashy televisions news. Like Warhol’s&nbsp; shoes, its disconnected, more imaginary than real. The Marxist thinker David Harvey writes more about&nbsp; the economic foundations of this depthlessness. If you study at the supply chains of any fast&nbsp; fashion company, any tech company, in fact,&nbsp;&nbsp; the majority of consumer goods, you’ll find&nbsp; that its fractured, outsourced, subcontracted,&nbsp;&nbsp; divided into small parts and&nbsp; separate companies across the globe,&nbsp;&nbsp; a button made here, a screen there, a&nbsp; screw in one place and a thread in another. For Harvey and Jameson, these facts of&nbsp; material production – how the economy&nbsp;&nbsp; is structured - is the reason the culture that&nbsp; results from it is so shallow. It doesn’t have&nbsp;&nbsp; time to be anything but and its constantly pushing&nbsp; for new trends. By the time a story, news item,&nbsp;&nbsp; a television show, a piece of art, or even a topic&nbsp; of discussion is produced, the world is moving on,&nbsp;&nbsp; manufacturing new product lines&nbsp; in new places based on new ideas. Harvey sees our postmodern consumer&nbsp; society as a result of the shift from&nbsp;&nbsp; Fordism – vertically integrated factories&nbsp; all owned and controlled by a single company&nbsp;&nbsp; overseeing each part of the process - to&nbsp; what he calls ‘flexible accumulation.’ Flexible accumulation is defined by outsourcing&nbsp; and subcontracting to break up the process&nbsp;&nbsp; into smaller bits, offsetting risks, making&nbsp; smaller companies to compete with one another&nbsp;&nbsp; for contracts so as to get the lowest price,&nbsp; being able to drop a manufacturer and hire a&nbsp;&nbsp; new one as soon as needed, when a style or trend&nbsp; changes. This leads a fractured economic system&nbsp;&nbsp; across the globe and a fractured culture as&nbsp; a result. New communication technologies,&nbsp;&nbsp; GPS, data centres, electronic banking, etc add&nbsp; to the speed and flexibility of the system. Harvey writes that ‘the mobilization of fashion&nbsp; in mass (as opposed to elite) markets provided&nbsp;&nbsp; a means to accelerate the pace of consumption&nbsp; not only in clothing, ornament, and decoration&nbsp;&nbsp; but also across a wide swathe of life-styles&nbsp; and recreational activities (leisure and&nbsp;&nbsp; sporting habits, pop music styles, video&nbsp; and children's games, and the like).’ And so lifestyles are adopted&nbsp; and discarded at the same rate as&nbsp;&nbsp; new trends, nothing is around long&nbsp; enough to be examined, understood,&nbsp;&nbsp; or identified with in any depth – we&nbsp; become detached, postmodern, lost. Fashion trends are adopted, mimicked, stolen, and&nbsp; ripped off; fads and countercultures are co-opted,&nbsp;&nbsp; profited from, then discarded. ‘All that&nbsp; is solid melts into air,’ as Marx wrote. Everything is disposable,&nbsp; single use - napkins, cups,&nbsp;&nbsp; cameras, batteries, and pens&nbsp; are used up and thrown away. Because everything is fast a quick turnover in&nbsp; images follows. Sponsorship, television styles,&nbsp;&nbsp; new cars, new styles in cinema and&nbsp; literature, new memes and new celebrities. Harvey illustrates how this shift between&nbsp; integrated Fordist factories and global&nbsp;&nbsp; flexible accumulation has effected our&nbsp; culture with the proliferation of galleries.&nbsp;&nbsp; He says that in New York in 1945 there&nbsp; were just a handful of gallioers. Now,&nbsp;&nbsp; 150,000 artist in New York claim&nbsp; professioanl status. There are&nbsp;&nbsp; 680 galleries producing more than 15&nbsp; million art works across a decade. They’re all bound up in the production of new&nbsp; images that can be exchanged and co-opted by our&nbsp;&nbsp; consumer culture which ultimately is about&nbsp; moving things on as quickly as possible. The problem, he says, is ‘Capital flight,&nbsp;&nbsp; de industrialization of some regions,&nbsp; and the industrialization of others,&nbsp;&nbsp; the destruction of traditional working-class&nbsp; communities as power bases in class struggle.’ Ok, lets summarise. There are two critiques.&nbsp; The one we just covered is about alienation,&nbsp;&nbsp; about us psychologically. That there’s&nbsp; a depthless, everything is surface,&nbsp;&nbsp; everything moves too quickly, and, according&nbsp; to many, we’re alienated from our true needs,&nbsp;&nbsp; from the true use value of objects and goods. This&nbsp; is a kind humanist critique. It focuses on us. The other critique is somewhat simpler. It’s&nbsp; that consumerism is destroying the planet,&nbsp;&nbsp; the environment. That consumerism is&nbsp; bad not per se, but because of appalling&nbsp;&nbsp; work conditions and labour rights and&nbsp; child labour in places like Bangladesh. I want to argue now that both can be seen as a&nbsp;&nbsp; type of depthlessness – and asking&nbsp; the question ‘what’s the opposite&nbsp;&nbsp; of depthlessness?’ - what would depth mean?&nbsp; Might help point us in the right direction. This humanist problem – the problem, essentially,&nbsp; of alienation – has been criticised by people&nbsp;&nbsp; who say alienation from what? Is there really&nbsp; any true authentic self to be alienated from?&nbsp;&nbsp; Aren’t we all the product of self-creation,&nbsp;&nbsp; an assemblage of experiences, differing&nbsp; from person to person, place to place. This is Douglas Kellner’s critique&nbsp; of Baudrillard – that he says we’re&nbsp;&nbsp; surrounded by image and sign and a&nbsp; hyperreality that alienates from the&nbsp;&nbsp; real of existence, but he posits no way out,&nbsp; no theory of change. If consumerism alienates&nbsp;&nbsp; but there is no true self anyway, on&nbsp; what basis can consumerism be wrong? I think this is true, but it doesn’t mean&nbsp; we can’t be alienated from our true needs,&nbsp;&nbsp; that certain things have a negative effect on us&nbsp; and the world, and other things a better effect.&nbsp;&nbsp; That some states of affairs in the&nbsp; world are more desirable than others. I want to quickly draw from two philosophers&nbsp; – Sartre & Spinoza - to make the case that to&nbsp;&nbsp; challenge the negatives of consumerism,&nbsp; we should aim to turn the depthlessness&nbsp;&nbsp; that is central to critiques&nbsp; of it into its opposite: depth.&nbsp;&nbsp; In turn, we aim to turn an alienated&nbsp; life into a more fulfilling one. The anthropologist Mary Douglas&nbsp; wrote that the ‘main problem of&nbsp;&nbsp; social life is to pin down meanings so&nbsp; that they stay still for a little time.’ Whether its fast moving images or our clothes&nbsp; being made by children thousands of miles away,&nbsp;&nbsp; this idea holds. There’s so much going on&nbsp; that it’s impossible to understand it all,&nbsp;&nbsp; to pin it down – and so in many areas we live&nbsp; shallowly, not understanding, not thinking,&nbsp;&nbsp; not able to fully comprehend what goes into&nbsp; the construction of our every day lives. So how do we pin down our fast moving&nbsp; consumer culture to analyse it in depth? Spinoza suggested that we look at&nbsp; the world from what we described as&nbsp;&nbsp; the perspective of eternity. We should examine&nbsp; the causes of things – where they come from,&nbsp;&nbsp; how they function, we should always analyse our&nbsp; ideas, actions, and desires, looking outwards&nbsp;&nbsp; and understanding them in the wider context of&nbsp; the world. We should look at things, essentially,&nbsp;&nbsp; in depth. We should understand where our food and&nbsp; clothes come from and the effect their having. And the French existentialist Jean-Paul Sartre&nbsp; made a similar point. He argued that our projects,&nbsp;&nbsp; our ideas, our opinions, and values – our&nbsp; perspective on the world – should rhyme. We should&nbsp;&nbsp; look at how things inform and effect one another. He argues that our experiences should together in&nbsp;&nbsp; a structure of meaning that we then impose&nbsp; onto the world. Meaning can be made deeper,&nbsp;&nbsp; more connected, more, well, meaningful, by&nbsp; uncovering and creating patterns between&nbsp;&nbsp; things so that the world rhymes, so&nbsp; that there’s rhythm and coherence.&nbsp; So if I make Youtube videos, I&nbsp; become interested in cameras to film,&nbsp;&nbsp; but I also then become interested in photography,&nbsp; and in how and where my cameras are made,&nbsp;&nbsp; what other things I can do with them,&nbsp; the history and philosophy of them.&nbsp; These are brief references to two philosophers&nbsp; I’ve introduced in depth before on the channel,&nbsp;&nbsp; but I think they get at something that shines a&nbsp; light on the depthlessness of consumer culture.&nbsp;&nbsp; And they help with a problem I think thinkers&nbsp; like Jameson and Baudrillard run into.&nbsp; After reading them you have the&nbsp; impression that consumerism is one&nbsp;&nbsp; totalising thing thing, everything gets lumped&nbsp; in with it – everything is just consumed and all&nbsp;&nbsp; images and adverts and consumer goods are equally&nbsp; negative and equally alienating. It ignores that&nbsp;&nbsp; not all things are consumed ‘shallowly’, some are&nbsp; experienced, approached, and consumed with depth. I buy new cameras and microphones,&nbsp; books, a drone, clothes, new foods,&nbsp;&nbsp; seek new recipes and holidays – precisely because&nbsp; they bring me the opposite of depthlessness,&nbsp;&nbsp; they create depth in my life. So to finish,&nbsp; lets have look at how depth is created, but&nbsp;&nbsp; what the limits of this way of&nbsp; thinking in this way might be. Sassatelli argues that often, rather than&nbsp; simply consuming brainlessly, consumers are&nbsp;&nbsp; active in the act of consumption. They’re&nbsp; also often decodifying, reinterpreting, and&nbsp;&nbsp; criticizing the PR, adverts, and products&nbsp; they consume. We’re not just zombies,&nbsp;&nbsp; taken in by every advertising board we see. She writes that ‘consumption often consists&nbsp; in re-framing the meaning and uses of material&nbsp;&nbsp; culture by translating the purely commercial value&nbsp; of goods into other forms of value: affection,&nbsp;&nbsp; relationships, symbolism, status, normality, etc,’ She continues ‘recent studies of audiences and&nbsp; media consumption show that spectators actively&nbsp;&nbsp; de-codify messages and images, referring them&nbsp; to the context in which they are experienced,&nbsp;&nbsp; to their own social position,&nbsp; gender, life course, and so on.’ Take DIY. Yes, new tools and paints and furniture&nbsp; are advertised and sold to us, but they’re often&nbsp;&nbsp; decommodified, made personal, adapted, decorated&nbsp; and adorned with family photos or meaningful&nbsp;&nbsp; items. There is a ‘de-commoditized sphere’ in the&nbsp; home, or between friends, at events and online. We use musical instruments to create&nbsp; new, individual, unique music, we&nbsp;&nbsp; paint and discuss and trade on social&nbsp; media, we fill photo books, we give&nbsp;&nbsp; gifts – all of these things transcend the flatness&nbsp; of consumerism and bring in more personal, social,&nbsp;&nbsp; ethical, or transcendental ideals. In 1970, Baudrillard pointed to the typewriter&nbsp; that can write in 13 different fonts and a&nbsp;&nbsp; diction machine to record notes as examples of&nbsp; pointless gadgets. To me, these seem useful – I&nbsp;&nbsp; use different fonts to convey different ideas&nbsp; or emotional tone quickly – its another layer to&nbsp;&nbsp; language. And others find recording to remember&nbsp; important things easier than jotting them down. Sassatelli also points to how&nbsp; the Walkman was criticized when&nbsp;&nbsp; it was first released for representing&nbsp; ‘aleination, anomie, and atomization’&nbsp;&nbsp; despite listening to music on the go clearly&nbsp; also being representative of many other&nbsp;&nbsp; things – escape, heightened experience,&nbsp; resistance, creativity, energy. She also writes about the positive experience&nbsp; of connoissuership, of collectibles, of hobbies: ‘the pervasive allure of connoisseurship may be&nbsp; seen as having to do with mastering objects and&nbsp;&nbsp; demonstrating aestheticized detachment from&nbsp; them: by piling up a complex repertoire of&nbsp;&nbsp; knowledge, the connoisseur finds&nbsp; a way to get close to commodities&nbsp;&nbsp; while distancing him or herself&nbsp; from their immediate hold.‘ Others have pointed to cinema, television,&nbsp; and image being deeper than is often assumed. In his book on Baudrillard, Adam Roberts&nbsp; writes that for Baudrillard Vietnam was&nbsp;&nbsp; ‘a war flattened and emptied out to a basic layer&nbsp; of violence, mixed in with popular culture and TV,&nbsp;&nbsp; accompanied in many people’s imagination&nbsp; by a soundtrack of 1960s pop-music.&nbsp;&nbsp; But the violence and death was not&nbsp; ‘hyper-real’ or ‘simulated’, it was real.’ My point is, in among the problems&nbsp; we’ve identified with consumer society,&nbsp;&nbsp; everywhere we look we can also find depth,&nbsp; meaning, usefulness, creativity, connection&nbsp;&nbsp; too. And we can apply this seeking after&nbsp; depth to our understanding of how things like&nbsp;&nbsp; supply chains work, what we think is&nbsp; unethical and ethical, what we want to support&nbsp;&nbsp; and avoid, what we want to push to regulate,&nbsp; organise against, and politically change.&nbsp;&nbsp; I think this is the opposite of&nbsp; depthlessness, the opposite of alienation. But am I being naive? Am I ignoring other&nbsp; issues? The breadth and scope of the problem.&nbsp;&nbsp; The addiction to new fashions, pointless&nbsp; new purchases, pollution or child labour? I guess, at least in part, what I’m arguing is&nbsp; that if you look at the consequences of your&nbsp;&nbsp; purchases in depth, if you think about the&nbsp; message, the result, the meaning in your own&nbsp;&nbsp; and other’s lives, then you can become&nbsp; an ethical consumer. Is this true? Even as that term ‘ethical consumption’ has&nbsp; become more popular, as we’ve become increasingly&nbsp;&nbsp; adware of the pitfalls of fast fashion and the&nbsp; environmental desegregation of consumption,&nbsp;&nbsp; Bottled water sales, to take&nbsp; just one simple example,&nbsp;&nbsp; have continued to rise and are projected&nbsp; to to so indefinitely. Palm oil – a major&nbsp;&nbsp; cause of deforestation - is still in half&nbsp; of packaged products. Fast fashion companies&nbsp;&nbsp; continue to pay below the minimum wage.&nbsp; Garment factories continue to burn down. But working out whether more conscious&nbsp; consumerism works at all is difficult to do. On the one hand, we continue to outsource to&nbsp; Bangladesh and see these tragedies that are&nbsp;&nbsp; the result of poor health and safety, terrible&nbsp; regulations, and labour practices, but at the&nbsp;&nbsp; same time, the ILO – the International Labour&nbsp; Organisation – says that child labour is down&nbsp;&nbsp; by a third since 2000. 61% of fashion companies&nbsp; have committed to using sustainable fabrics. That is, when there’s cultural&nbsp; pressure on manufacturers,&nbsp;&nbsp; on what we eat and wear there&nbsp; does appear to be some change. On the other hand, NorthWestern&nbsp; University professor Brayden King&nbsp;&nbsp; has argued boycotts have a negligible effect&nbsp; on a companies sales revenue. He says that the&nbsp;&nbsp; problem is “we can’t pay attention to&nbsp; any single controversy for very long.” Yes, we talk about the tragic Rana Plaze&nbsp; building collapse in Bangladesh in 2013 when&nbsp;&nbsp; 1134 died for a bit, but then&nbsp; we move on to the other things. Terry Hathaway at the LSE writes that ‘Even the&nbsp; most hyper-vigilant, well-informed shopper cannot&nbsp;&nbsp; know everything – the labour (and conditions),&nbsp; the tools (and the production of these tools),&nbsp;&nbsp; the raw materials (and their extraction), the&nbsp; energy, etc. – that goes into making even the most&nbsp;&nbsp; simple products. Instead, the consumer must buy in&nbsp; partial ignorance of all of the factors, primarily&nbsp;&nbsp; on the basis of those attributes that are the most&nbsp; conspicuous and, to some degree, based on trust.’ He continues ‘shopping at Whole Foods could be&nbsp; construed as support for higher welfare meat&nbsp;&nbsp; and organic agricultural methods,&nbsp; but it will equally support&nbsp;union&nbsp;&nbsp; busting,&nbsp;low wages&nbsp;for workers&nbsp; and&nbsp;right-wing libertarian politics.’ So here is the crux of it. Our consumer society&nbsp; is messy, complex; it both sustains us creatively&nbsp;&nbsp; and destroys the planet. So maybe it is a&nbsp; useless concept. I think we’re better off&nbsp;&nbsp; thinking about it in its original sense – to use&nbsp; up – as, not a noun that describes our soceity,&nbsp;&nbsp; but as a verb -as something we’re all doing. And&nbsp; like anything we do, there is a chain of activity,&nbsp;&nbsp; social and historical, environmental and economic&nbsp; – that supports the consumption and that we in&nbsp;&nbsp; turn support by consuming. Only by studying the&nbsp; understanding the issues in depth can we grapple&nbsp;&nbsp; with these problems. Thinking about regulation,&nbsp; changing the economic system, organising&nbsp;&nbsp; politically is a part of this depth – everyone’s&nbsp; interpretation of what to do will be different. For example, journalist Alden Wicker&nbsp; argues ethical consumption doesn’t work.&nbsp;&nbsp; We should instead donate some of&nbsp; the money we spend going greener&nbsp;&nbsp; on donations to NGOs and green politicians. And commentator Robert Reich has reminded&nbsp; us that when “you hear a company boast about&nbsp;&nbsp; how environmentally friendly it is, hold the&nbsp; applause. Under super-competitive capitalism—what&nbsp;&nbsp; I’ve termed ‘supercapitalism’—it’s&nbsp; naive to think corporations can or&nbsp;&nbsp; will sacrifice profits and shareholder&nbsp; returns in order to fight global warming.&nbsp;&nbsp; Firms that go green to improve their&nbsp; public relations, or cut their costs,&nbsp;&nbsp; or anticipate regulations are&nbsp; being smart, not virtuous.” So its important to approach this&nbsp; with a multifaceted attitude.&nbsp;&nbsp; Depth means more eyes on all the issues.&nbsp; Depth means engaging with the politics. Depth&nbsp;&nbsp; means exploring our own desires and beliefs&nbsp; vigilantly. Taking an issue – something we&nbsp;&nbsp; consume - and understanding the ramifications,&nbsp; something I want to try to apply next time.

- The importance of studying consumer behavior: Kind: captions Language: en Okay, let's do this. Today, I'm going to teach you what consumer behavior is. First of all, it is defined as the area of research within the field of marketing that focuses on how consumers acquire, use, and dispose of goods, services, time, and ideas. Consumers can be individuals, families, or other groups such as teams and companies. Let's try to understand the importance of studying consumer behavior. Suppose you need a new phone. How would you go about satisfying this need? Where would you turn to for information? How would you set your budget? Where would you buy the phone? These are just some decisions consumers face on a regular basis. Interestingly, each consumer will answer these questions differently based on their backgrounds and some psychological factors. For a company that makes phones, the answers to these questions will help them know the types of phones to design, the price consumers are willing to pay, and where they should sell their phones. It is very important to understand how consumers make decisions because the best way to create and keep customers is to understand what motivates their consumption decisions and anticipate their consumption needs. Only this way, companies can design products, services, and offers that will make their customers happy. [Applause] [Music]

First of all, understanding where the other side's coming from and especially emotionally, and then being able to feed it back to them in a way that they signal to you that you've got it right. Understand and demonstrate that understanding. There are a lot of negotiators that really will give in on a deal because being understood is more important than getting what they want. So once we completely understand where somebody's coming from, then with tactical empathy, we get a much better feel for exactly how they feel about things, how that drives them- and then how we can interact with the things that are driving them. The reasons you won't make a deal are typically more important than the reasons you will make a deal. There's Nobel Prize-winning behavioral economics theory that says that people will put a value of losses on at least twice what an equivalent gain is. So losing $5 stings at least twice as much as gaining $5. Losing $5 feels like losing $10 or even $35- it's just a ridiculous skewing in our brains over loss. So knowing that fear of loss is probably going to drive someone's decision-making more than anything else, tactically, I want to diffuse those fears. I want to get them out of that fear-based thinking, and I want to get them really in a more rational, open frame of mind as quickly as I can, which is why, tactically and empathy, I wanna address their fears first. Well, labeling is the best way to practice tactical empathy: In its strictest form, it's just saying, or writing, "it seems like, it sounds like, it looks like," putting a label on the dynamic. And science is showing us now, that if we label a negative, it diminishes it. I'll actually say to somebody ahead of time, "Look, this is gonna sound really harsh, and there's a really good chance that when I get done saying what I'm gonna say, you're not gonna like me at all." - The Psychology Behind Good Advertising: Kind: captions Language: en It should come as no surprise that modern advertising as we know it, has shaped our society in many ways. A lot of our daily decisions and life choices are influenced in part by advertising itself. It’s become such a deep-rooted constituent of our established norm that a world without it would seem, frankly, strange "Like so many others, I had become a slave to the IKEA nesting instinct" "Uh, yes. I'd like to order the Erica Pekkary dust ruffles" "Please hold." This is because barely a moment goes by during our day when we aren’t bombarded with advertisements in some form or the other. Posters, billboards, flyers, TV commercials, and internet ads, all creep into our personal space and tell us what we should buy and who we should be. For now our only brief escape from our role as a potential consumer comes to us during sleep. But even this could possibly change one day. "Are you bored?" "Get Sky Go for your mobile" "Best entertainment and live sport" "When you want it and where you want it" What's important to know is that the purpose of advertising isn’t limited in its capacity to harass us into parting with our hard earned money. Advertising plays a traditional role in helping businesses reach prospective customers and vice versa. Without it we would not know where to look for a particular product or service we need. Perhaps without advertising we wouldn’t even know what we wanted in the first place. Yet in our present day technologically driven lives, the reach between producer and consumer has grown a lot smaller. With the numerous media platforms and channels available to us, a simple online search takes us to a list of providers able to satisfy our every want. Our dilemma today comes in the form of not knowing which product to choose from out of the many available to us. This is where good advertising comes into play. In a saturated market, subtle differences can make the distinction between the choice of one product over another. There are typically two modes of advertising that ad agencies and marketing gurus utilize. One focuses on the qualities of the product, while the other seeks to arouse an emotional response from the intended audience. The moment you start to think about advertisements that have stood out to you in the recent past, there’s a high probability that they incorporated the latter. And there’s a good reason for this. "Well gentlemen, I don't think I have to tell you what you just witnessed here" "I think you do" Why should you choose one product over another? That decision becomes easy when you develop an affinity with a particular brand. It could be something as small as an aesthetically appealing logo design. Something that resonates with you and feels calming. The right colours and appropriate typography all matched in harmony for a well packaged product. But advertising goes beyond a well thought out logo or attractive packaging. The most successful ad campaigns hardly say anything about the product itself but instead create a lucid atmosphere that evokes a strong emotion from its target consumer. These are the types of advertisements that we remember, talk about, and influence our purchasing decisions. Now, let’s take a look at the following two commercials about perfume: "Fragrances by Shulton" "The essence of precious scents caught in that precise moment of fulfillment" "Distilled with exquisite artistry for your every mood" "In four fragrances" "Here's the newest adventure in fragrances" "Escapade" "A blending of subtle French genius with a bold, vivacious, American touch" "To be lovely is to feel lovely when your fragrance expresses your gayest self" "So choose a gay adventure - choose Escapade toilet water" "Immediately, you'll feel lovely" "Why, you are lovely in that light and gay Escapade mood" "And remember your Escapade stick cologne to a new adventure, wherever you are" "Enjoy all these fragrances" "Friendship's garden" "Early American Old Spice" "Dessert Flower - At leading cosmetic counters everywhere" "Toilet Waters at a $1.25 and a $1.50, stick colognes $1" "Acqua di Gioia, the new eau fraiche" "Giorgio Armani" The differences between the two commercials are quite stark. The first ad for Escapade Perfume quite explicitly focuses on the product itself. They describe certain characteristics of the perfume while going on to talk about its application and effect on the user. And this is quite difficult to do when describing a product whose main selling attribute (smell) is not transmissible through Television. It almost seems absurd, but the second perfume commercial for Giorgio Armani does not even try in the least to directly communicate the features of their product. They rely solely on alighting particular feelings and associations with their perfume. In this case, we could assume that the directors behind the ad wanted to transmit the feeling of ethereal beauty. We see a woman who fits into our standard of high attractiveness in our society, frolicking through a rainforest in the midst of a storm. The only mention of the perfume is in the last six seconds of the one minute ad. So why do we care about the associations of a product, rather than the product itself? Good advertising helps us begin to answer one of the most fundamental questions of life – Who Am I? This is because when it comes to figuring out who we are and what we want from life, we usually struggle to find answers. A lot of this is existential and has to do with the fact that we’re born with no pre-established notion of what it means to be human. It’s up to us to figure that along the way. But making that decision isn’t easy. In fact, it’s a huge burden. Out of all the possibilities our lives can take, how can we decide who or what we should be? We have no inkling if the choices we make will turn out to be good or not. Yet, we are each tasked with the responsibility of deciding for ourselves and can only hope that we’ve chosen well. On the other hand, good advertising helps us build an identity by releasing the anxiety brought about by self-determination. It tells us exactly what choice to make by compelling us to buy a certain product. And once we have done so, we will be able to emulate the identity and characteristics that we have learned to associate with that product from a particular commercial or advertisement. "Advertising is based on one thing" "Happiness" "And do you know what happiness is? Happiness is the smell of a new car" "It's freedom from fear. It's a billboard on the side of the road that screams, with reassurance, that whatever you're doing, it's okay." "You are okay" Advertising that caters to our feelings, primarily resonates with our subconscious mind and not our conscious mind. It’s why we sometimes can’t rationally deduce our preference for a certain brand and our ability to pay a premium for a product we can’t tell apart from its competitors. If we are drawn to it simply because of what it evokes inside of us and the associations that come with it, then rest assured, the marketing department has done their research. What this means is that we need to start thinking carefully about the decisions we make even if it’s something as insignificant as purchasing a perfume. Good advertising feeds off both our insecurities and deficiencies as humans and makes us believe that we can mask them with a new and exciting identity. Make no mistake, the only thing you’ll be able to achieve is to diminish your anxiety in the short term. And of course, you’ll spend money on things you don’t need in order to quell a discomfort that needs to be addressed appropriately. Making authentic decisions that align with our best interests is no easy task and takes a lot of effort. Yet, we have to realize that losing ourselves into the illusions constructed by good advertising will not make our lives any easier. They will only detract us from accepting and being comfortable with who we really are and the givens of our reality. There is no point striving towards an ideal when perfection doesn’t exist. Accomplish this and you’ll be a much happier individual.

- What Neuromarketing Insights Can fMRI Provide? - Neurotech Insight Pro: Kind: captions Language: en What neuromarketing insights can fMRI provide? Imagine being able to see what happens inside a person's brain when they see your product or ad. That is what functional magnetic resonance imaging or fMRI makes possible. It measures blood flow in the brain, showing which areas become active during specific tasks or stimuli. In neuromarketing, this tool offers a direct look at how consumers respond to marketing messages, revealing reactions that traditional surveys might miss. Unlike asking people what they think, fMRI captures real-time brain activity even when people are unaware of their true feelings. This makes it a powerful way to understand the subconscious drivers behind buying decisions. One of the key benefits of fMRI is its ability to predict behavior. For example, if certain brain regions light up when someone looks at a product, it can suggest whether they are likely to buy it. Studies have shown that patterns of brain activity can forecast if a person will respond positively to an advertisement or if they will prefer one brand over another. This predictive aspect helps marketers fine-tune their campaigns before they go live, saving time and money. Marketers often use fMRI to test different commercials. By scanning viewers brains while they watch, they can see which ads trigger the strongest emotional or motivational responses. This helps identify the most effective messages to boost engagement. Similarly, concept testing with fMRI shows which ideas resonate most deeply with consumers, guiding campaign development. Branding is another area where fMRI provides valuable insights. By analyzing how the brain reacts to different brand elements, companies can create a neuro brand signature, a unique neural pattern linked to their brand. Tracking the signature over time reveals how marketing efforts influence consumer perceptions. Packaging design also benefits from fMRI as it can show which visual elements attract attention and encourage purchases. For example, bright colors or familiar imagery might activate specific brain areas associated with positive feelings or recognition. Some researchers combine fMRI with eye tracking to get a fuller picture. IT tracking shows where people look and for how long, while fMRI reveals how those visual cues affect brain activity. This combination helps marketers understand not just what catches the eye, but also what truly influences the mind. Following up neural scans with interviews adds context, helping explain why certain stimuli evoke specific reactions. In the broader field of brain mapping and diagnostics, fMRI's ability to visualize brain responses to marketing stimuli highlights how neurodenology extends beyond medicine. It offers a new way to understand consumer behavior on a neural level. While the technology is still costly and complex, ongoing improvements and decreasing costs could make fMRI more accessible in the future. This could lead to more personalized and effective marketing strategies tailored to how individual brains respond. Overall, fMRI provides a window into the subconscious mind, revealing what truly motivates consumers. It bridges the gap between observable actions and the neural processes behind them, offering insights that can shape smarter, more targeted marketing efforts. As neurodechnology advances, tools like fMRI will likely become even more important in understanding how the brain influences buying choices and brand loyalty.
